papers.title: Paintable In Situ Gelling Bioelectronic Interfaces for Epidermal Electrophysiological Monitoring.
papers.abstract: Noninvasive epidermal electrophysiological monitoring is frequently constrained by unstable electrode-skin contact interfaces over soft, textured, and dynamically deforming skin. The predefined geometries of conventional electrodes limit their capacity to conform to local microtopography. Here, we introduce an in situ gelation strategy performed directly on the epidermis to construct a conformal ionic bioelectronic interface. A fluidic precursor comprising gelatin and tannic acid is initially stabilized against premature gelation via competitive solvent-solute interactions. Upon application, solvent evaporation and gelatin reassembly induce rapid network formation. This process directly yields a highly conformal and gently detachable interface with remarkably low contact impedance. The resulting hydrated dynamic network provides mechanical compliance, robust interfacial adhesion, stretch-tolerant ionic conduction, and cooling-induced interfacial weakening that enables gentle removal. The on-skin-gelled interface reduces skin-electrode contact impedance to 30 kΩ at 10 Hz, compared with 191 kΩ for commercial conductive pastes, and increases the signal-to-noise ratio from 24.9 to 27.8 dB. In proof-of-concept demonstrations, the interface supports within-subject electromyography-based gesture recognition with a classification accuracy of 93.4% and electroencephalography recordings of eye-state-dependent α-rhythm modulation as well as short-term sleep-related waveforms. These findings underscore the potential of on-skin in situ gelation as a versatile approach to fabricating paintable ionic bioelectronic interfaces for advanced electrophysiological monitoring.

papers.title: Sex- and age-specific daily and seasonal rhythms in haemoglobin and ferritin among Dutch blood donors.
papers.abstract: Intra-individual haemoglobin (Hb) and ferritin variation is often overlooked in clinical practice, yet may be relevant where levels are around the cut-offs. We characterised Hb and ferritin fluctuations across the year and day in Dutch blood donors. We included 337,218 capillary Hb (cHb) and 171,542 serum ferritin measurements routinely collected between 8:00 AM and 9:00 PM in new blood donors aged 18-65 years. Cosinor rhythms with 24-h and 12-month periods were fitted for males and females separately. Donor groups were stratified into <45 and ≥45 years of age as a proxy for the onset of menopause and age-related changes in circadian physiology. cHb levels showed a 24-h rhythm, peaking around 10:30 AM. The daily amplitude was larger for males (0.122 mmol/L) than females (0.093 mmol/L), but females ≥45 years had a larger amplitude (0.106 mmol/L) than those <45. The cHb peak time occurred earlier in donors ≥45 (around 9:40 AM) than those <45 (around 10:40 AM). cHb levels were higher in winter than in summer. The yearly amplitude was larger in males (0.036 mmol/L) than in females (0.020 mmol/L). Ferritin levels also peaked in winter with similar amplitude in males and females. The cosinor behaviour of cHb levels during the day may indicate contribution of circadian physiology. An earlier cHb peak time in older donors agrees with the known association between 'morningness' and older age. These results support the interpretation of cHb and ferritin measurements in clinical practice and may fuel further research into underlying mechanisms.

papers.title: Structural basis of ligand recognition and gating in mosquito IRs.
papers.abstract: Ionotropic receptors (IRs) are essential for insect olfaction, enabling the detection of carboxylic acids, amines, moisture, and temperature cues that mediate critical behaviors, including mosquito host-seeking 1,2. However, the structural mechanisms underlying ligand specificity and channel activation in these receptors remain unclear. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures and functional validation of the IR8a-IR75k complex from the malaria mosquito Anopheles stephensi, a carboxylic acid detector, captured in four states: the ligand-free full-length closed form (apo state), the ligand induced full-length open state, and the nonanoic acid (NA)- and octanoic acid (OA)-bound extracellular domains. These structures reveal a dynamic ligand-binding pocket in IR75k, in which specificity is determined by alkyl chain length and carboxylate geometry. Ligand binding triggers closure of IR75k's bilobed ligand binding domain (LBD), and this conformational change propagates through conserved mechanical linkers to the transmembrane domain (TMD), functioning as a molecular lever that dilates the pore via outward displacement of transmembrane helices. This gating mechanism was further corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations and electrophysiology. These insights provide an atomic resolution view of IR mediated host detection in mosquitoes and establish a foundation for the rational design of next generation mosquito control strategies targeting host-seeking behavior.

papers.title: Lesions in the cerebellum impact cross-modal temporal predictions.
papers.abstract: The cerebellum (CE) supports the encoding of the precise sensory event timing and the generation of temporal predictions. Here we investigated whether focal CE lesions impact temporal predictions in a cross-modal context. Individuals with CE lesion (n=9) and healthy-matched controls (HC) were presented with visuo-auditory stimulus pairs, presented in a temporally regular (predictable) or irregular (unpredictable) manner while EEG was recorded. We hypothesized cross-modal temporal predictions to be mediated by pre-stimulus cerebello-cortical beta-band (12-25Hz) activity. In turn, we expected HC, but not CE patients, to show a modulation of pre-stimulus beta power as a function of temporal prediction. HC showed greater pre-stimulus beta-band suppression presumably related to anticipation of sound onsets, and stronger post-stimulus delta-band (1-4Hz) power in the predictable than unpredictable condition. Furthermore, they displayed a significant modulation of pre-stimulus delta-beta cross-frequency coupling as a function of temporal predictability. These effects were not observed in the CE group, suggesting a deficit in temporal predictions. These results extend the role of cerebellar predictive timing from sensorimotor to motor-independent cross-modal temporal predictions.

papers.title: A homozygous GABRA2 variant associated with infantile spasms evolving to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome alters receptor gating.
papers.abstract: Variants in GABAA receptor subunits are increasingly implicated in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. Although GABRA2 variants have been associated with early-onset epilepsy, the functional consequences of individual variants, particularly those located outside canonical ligand-binding and transmembrane pore-forming regions, remain incompletely understood. We identified a homozygous GABRA2p.A407K variant in a patient with infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS) evolving to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS). Functional effects were assessed using two-electrode voltage clamp in Xenopus laevis oocytes and whole-cell patch clamp recordings in HEK293T cells expressing α2β3γ2 GABAA receptors. A Gabra2p.A407K/A407K knock-in mouse model was generated to examine neuronal membrane properties, provoked seizure responses, and behavioral phenotypes. The p.A407K variant did not impair receptor trafficking but slowed receptor desensitization. In hippocampal slices from adult knock-in mice, CA1 pyramidal neurons exhibited a more depolarized resting membrane potential and were positioned closer to action potential threshold, while action potential threshold itself was unchanged. In a limited adult EEG cohort of Gabra2p.A407K/A407K mice, no spontaneous seizures or overt epileptiform activity were detected. However, mutant mice showed prolonged seizure duration following 6 Hz corneal stimulation. Behavioral analyses revealed increased locomotor activity and altered exploratory behavior. These findings show that a rare homozygous GABRA2 intracellular loop variant alters α2-containing GABAA receptor gating and produces measurable neuronal, behavioral, and provoked seizure-response effects in a knock-in mouse model. The model does not reproduce the full human developmental epileptic encephalopathy phenotype but supports the conclusion that p.A407K is functionally consequential and provides a platform for studying variant-specific effects of GABRA2 dysfunction.

papers.title: Short-term methionine starvation reshapes diurnal hepatic m6A RNA methylation.
papers.abstract: Dietary methionine restriction improves metabolic health and has therapeutic potential in multiple disease contexts. Methionine metabolism regulates transmethylation reactions, including N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA methylation, by modulating availability of S-adenosyl methionine (SAM). Both m6A methylation and methionine metabolism have separately been linked to circadian regulation, but whether dietary methionine influences circadian rhythms through m6A remains unknown. Here we show that short-term methionine deprivation induces diurnal variation in serum methionine and SAM and reprograms diurnal expression of m6A writers, erasers, and readers in mouse liver. Methylated RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (MeRIP-seq) at two timepoints (ZT9, ZT21) revealed that a methionine-deficient (MD) diet was associated with a roughly 10-fold increase in differentially methylated m6A peaks between timepoints relative to control, despite no change in methylation at core clock transcripts. These diet-induced oscillations arose at sites already methylated under the control diet, indicating that methionine restriction alters the rhythmicity of existing m6A marks rather than inducing new methylation, and were enriched in transcripts involved in RNA processing, translation, ubiquitination, and mTORC1 signaling. Integrating RNA-seq and proteomics, we found that a subset of these m6A changes co-occurred with altered mRNA and/or protein abundance, indicating gene-specific rather than global effects. Notably, reduced m6A methylation of Mat2a and Cbs, encoding enzymes central to methionine homeostasis, was associated with increased MAT2A and decreased CBS protein levels, respectively. These findings identify diet-induced, diurnally rhythmic m6A methylation as a candidate mechanism linking methionine metabolism to circadian biology and nominate specific m6A sites and pathways for future investigation.

papers.title: Caffeine Consumption and Adolescent Mental Health: The Role of Sleep and Brain Structure.
papers.abstract: Caffeine is a widely consumed psychoactive substance, with use beginning during adolescence, a sensitive period of neurodevelopment. Despite its widespread, unregulated use, links between caffeine consumption and adolescent brain structure and mental health remain poorly understood. We examined the association between caffeine intake and brain structure in 9632 adolescents aged 9-11 years. Caffeine consumption (intake of coffee, tea and soft drinks) and mental health were assessed via self-report. Cortical thickness and surface area were derived from structural MRI scans. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between caffeine intake and brain measures. Structural equation modeling was used to test whether sleep duration and brain structure mediated the association between caffeine intake and mental health outcomes assessed at the 6-month and 18-month follow-up. Higher total caffeine intake was associated with lower total cortical surface area (B=-0.03,SE=0.01,p=.001) and lower surface area in 22 regions across four lobes, driven largely by soft drink consumption, with some additional associations emerging for coffee and espresso intake with cortical thickness. All associations were evident at consumption levels as low as one cup per week. Shorter sleep duration and lower surface area sequentially mediated the association between higher caffeine intake and greater mental health problems in the future. Findings highlight the need for evidence-based guidelines on adolescent caffeine consumption to support neurodevelopment and mental health.
papers.journal: Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging

papers.title: Environmental enrichment preserves intestinal endocannabinoid signaling under LPS-inflammatory conditions.
papers.abstract: Environmental factors critically influence intestinal homeostasis, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying these effects remain incompletely understood. The endocannabinoid system (ECS), a key regulator of immune, metabolic, and epithelial functions, has emerged as a promising pharmacological target in inflammatory disorders. However, whether environmental context influences intestinal ECS signaling and the coordinated mechanisms underlying intestinal homeostasis during inflammation remains unclear. This study investigated the impact of environmental enrichment (EE) on intestinal ECS regulation in the context of impaired intestinal homeostasis during lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced systemic inflammation. Adult male mice were housed under standard or enriched conditions for four weeks before LPS challenge (830 μg/kg, i.p., 24 h). ECS receptors (Cnr1, Cnr2), ECS-related targets (Trpv1, Pparγ), metabolic enzymes (Nape-pld, Dagl-β, Faah, Magl), inflammatory mediators (Tlr4, Tnf-α, Il-6), epithelial barrier markers (Ocln, Zo-1), endocannabinoid levels (AEA and 2-AG), selected bacterial taxa, and microbiota-derived metabolites were evaluated in the proximal colon. LPS induced coordinated changes in the intestinal ECS-related measures, endocannabinoid levels, inflammatory signaling, barrier-associated markers, and the selected microbial-metabolic profile. EE mitigated several of these changes, including ECS-related transcriptional and protein alterations and local inflammatory responses, while modulating tight-junction proteins, selected fecal bacterial taxa, microbiota-derived metabolites, and the integrated multivariate profile. Overall, EE modulates intestinal response profile consistent with greater resilience to inflammatory stress across ECS, inflammatory, barrier-associated, and microbial-metabolic measures. These findings suggest that ECS regulation may represent a context-dependent determinant of responsiveness to ECS-targeting pharmacological interventions.

papers.title: Analysis choices can produce apparent rich-club differences: an Alzheimer's disease EEG case study.
papers.abstract: The weighted rich-club coefficient tests whether a network's most strongly connected nodes are preferentially interconnected. Its interpretation depends on two often-implicit choices: how the randomised comparison networks are constructed, and whether the hubs are re-identified in each comparison network or held fixed at those of the observed network. When hubs are defined by connection strength, these choices change what the coefficient tests. We examined how these choices affect inference using resting-state EEG from 20 people with Alzheimer's disease and 20 controls. Holding the data fixed, we compared four analysis pipelines, crossing two ways of building the comparison networks (global weight reshuffle or strength-conditioned null) with the two hub choices, and ran a calibration study using data constructed to contain no preferential hub coupling beyond nodal strength. An apparent eyes-open group difference in rich-club organisation appeared only under the pipeline combining a global weight reshuffle with re-identified hubs. Under the empirical resampling ensemble, that pipeline reported a group difference in 43% of pseudo-studies, always higher in the Alzheimer's disease group, while the other three stayed near the expected 5%. Unlike global weight reshuffling, strength-conditioned nulls approximately preserve nodal strengths; fixing observed hubs also retains the identity of the core being tested. The same data can support or dissolve an apparent rich-club difference depending on these choices. No single choice is universally correct, but reporting which were made, and why they fit the question being asked, is essential to interpreting the result.

papers.title: Pilot, Feasibility, and Acceptability Evaluation of a Mindfulness-Based Intervention with Diabetes Education in Adolescents with Type 1 Diabetes.
papers.abstract: Most adolescents living with type 1 diabetes (T1D) do not reach targeted levels of hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), which increases risk for diabetes-related complications. Suboptimal diabetes management may be associated with the burden of coping with T1D for adolescents who are simultaneously adjusting to physical, cognitive, and socioemotional changes. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are associated with improved coping skills and could be useful for adolescents with T1D. This was a pilot randomized controlled study to examine the feasibility and acceptability of a virtual MBI in adolescents aged 15-17 years with T1D. Enrollment took place in two iterations: 1) patients were approached in clinic by a physician; 2) letters were mailed and follow-up phone calls were made by research staff. Enrolled participants were given the option of 2 different weekly times for participation and were assigned to one of two study arms: diabetes education + MBI (DE+MBI) or DE only. For each arm, 12 virtual group sessions were held weekly. Feasibility measures included time-to-recruit, program enrollment, and study retention. Acceptability was assessed by attendance and survey completion. Exploratory outcomes included HbA1c and responses to quality of life and mental health questionnaires. By design, the first 60 eligible participants who agreed to participate were enrolled. Sixty of 164 approached (37%) consented to enroll. Fifty percent of these (n=30; DE+MBI=15, DE=15) participated in at least one group session; the mean attendance was 7 + 3 sessions. All participants reported managing at least one area of life better post-intervention (coping with stress, sleep, physical symptoms, self-care, school, emotion regulation, getting along with others). Survey completion was 87% pre-intervention and 60% post-intervention. There was no change in mean HbA1c for either the DE+MBI or the DE arms. More study is warranted to investigate ways to increase the feasibility for implementing complementary therapies such as MBI in a diabetes clinic for adolescents with T1D.

papers.title: Differences in neurovascular coupling in patients with major depressive disorder: Evidence from simultaneous resting-state EEG-fNIRS.
papers.abstract: Neurovascular coupling (NVC), the relationship between neural activity and cerebral hemodynamic responses, remains poorly understood in major depressive disorder (MDD). To investigate alterations in NVC associated with depressive symptom severity, we simultaneously recorded resting-state electroencephalography (rsEEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) in 206 participants, including 134 patients with MDD and 72 healthy controls stratified by age to disentangle disease-related alterations from age-associated effects. NVC in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) was characterized by the consistency and temporal lag between spontaneous electrophysiological peaks and corresponding hemodynamic responses. We found that age significantly enhances the NVC consistency (p < 0.05), whereas this relationship was altered in patients with MDD during both the oxygen-consumption phase and the subsequent hemodynamic compensation phase. Furthermore, among patients with MDD, the strength of this consistency decreased more significantly with greater illness severity (partial r = -0.336, p = 0.0601). These findings suggest that changes in neurovascular coupling effects are strongly associated with the severity of depression. By leveraging wearable neuroimaging techniques, this study provides multimodal evidence for altered neurovascular coupling in depression and highlights its potential as a biomarker for disease monitoring and recovery trajectories.

papers.title: Turning Back the Ageing Clock? Brain Age in Neuroprotective and Clinical Interventions.
papers.abstract: Neuroimaging-derived brain age has emerged as an intuitive marker of brain health and cognitive longevity. The difference between brain age and chronological age, termed brain-predicted age difference (brain-PAD), quantifies deviation from normative brain ageing and may help evaluate whether interventions could attenuate brain ageing trajectories. This review synthesizes the methodological foundations of brain age estimation, factors linked to brain-PAD across healthy ageing and disease, evidence from clinical interventions, and emerging translational applications in clinical trials. Across non-clinical and clinical populations, older-appearing brains are associated with poorer cognitive and physical function, greater physiological burden, higher mortality risk, cardiometabolic vulnerability, and a range of neurological and psychiatric disorders. Evidence from interventions remains limited and heterogeneous. Exercise provides the clearest proof-of-concept that brain-PAD is potentially modifiable, whereas dietary interventions and multidomain lifestyle programmes have produced suggestive but preliminary evidence; cognitive, sleep, and mind-body interventions have yielded sparse or mixed findings. In clinical settings, brain-PAD shows promise for predicting disease conversion, disability progression, and treatment response, and may support trial stratification, enrichment and monitoring. Evidence that medication, neuromodulation, or other interventions reliably normalize brain-PAD, however, remains inconsistent. We argue that brain-PAD is a useful but biologically nonspecific, model-derived biomarker. Its interpretation critically depends on pipeline choice, harmonization, age-bias correction, and longitudinal validity. For now, brain-PAD is best regarded as a complementary biomarker and exploratory outcome rather than a validated surrogate endpoint. Future progress will require standardized methods, validation in representative populations and prespecified longitudinal cohorts that links brain-age changes to meaningful clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Association of Sleep Duration with MASLD Status and Hepatic Steatosis Index in Korean Adults: The Indirect Role of Sedentary Behavior.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects nearly three in ten adults globally, while its prevalence in South Korea has risen by approximately 3-4% per year. Although MASLD is linked to lifestyle factors, few studies have examined the associations among sleep duration, MASLD status, and the hepatic steatosis index (HSI). Accordingly, we evaluated the relationship between sleep duration and MASLD status and separately assessed whether sedentary behavior formed an indirect pathway between sleep duration and HSI, an indicator of hepatic steatosis. The analysis included 26,909 adults aged 20 years or older who participated in the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey from 2014 through 2021. Logistic regression was used to estimate the relationship of sleep duration with MASLD status. Mediation analysis was conducted using HSI as the outcome variable to examine whether sedentary behavior indirectly linked sleep duration with HSI. MASLD was identified in 23.2% of 26,909 participants. In the adjusted logistic model, MASLD odds were higher among participants sleeping ≤4 hours (OR = 1.44, 95% CI: 1.17-1.78) and those reporting ≥8 hours of sedentary time (OR = 1.17, 95% CI: 1.09-1.25). Correlations of HSI with sleep duration (r = -.06, p < .001) and sedentary behavior (r = .02, p < .001) were small. The mediation model yielded a direct association between sleep duration and HSI (β = -0.21, 95% CI: -0.26 to -0.16), whereas the indirect effect through sedentary behavior was statistically significant but minimal (β = -0.0073, 95% bootstrap CI: -0.0118 to -0.0032). MASLD status was related to both shorter sleep and longer sedentary time. Nevertheless, the very small correlations among sleep duration, sedentary behavior, and HSI offered little empirical support for a meaningful mediation pathway. Longitudinal research is required to establish the direction and timing of these relationships.
keywords: Metabolic dysfunction associated steatotic liver disease

papers.title: Pain-Related Dysfunctional Beliefs About Sleep and Depression Mediate the Influence of Pain Severity on Fear of Progression Among Individuals With Cancer.
papers.abstract: This study investigated whether pain severity contributes meaningfully to fear of progression (FoP) among individuals with cancer and assessed the mediating roles of psychological symptoms, specifically pain-related dysfunctional beliefs about sleep and depressive symptoms, in this association. We retrospectively reviewed medical records of 252 individuals with cancer who attended the Sleep Clinic for cancer patients at Asan Medical Center. Demographic and clinical data were extracted alongside responses to self-report questionnaires, including the Fear of Progression Questionnaire-Short Form (FoP-Q-SF), Pain-Related Beliefs and Attitudes about Sleep (PBAS), Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), State subscale of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-S), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), and numeric pain rating scales. Pearson correlation and linear regression analyses were conducted to examine associations among variables, particularly the contribution of pain and psychological symptoms to FoP. Mediation analysis was performed using maximum likelihood regression. FoP-Q-SF scores were significantly positively correlated with pain (r=0.36, p<0.001), PBAS (r=0.43, p<0.001), ISI (r=0.25, p<0.001), PHQ-9 (r=0.66, p<0.001), and STAI-S (r=0.22, p<0.001). Linear regression analysis indicated that FoP-Q-SF scores were predicted by age (β=-0.28, p<0.001), pain (β=0.13, p=0.013), PBAS (β=0.15, p=0.007), and PHQ-9 (β=0.55, p<0.001). Mediation analysis demonstrated that pain exerted a direct effect on FoP-Q-SF scores, with both PBAS and PHQ-9 partially mediating this relationship. These findings suggest that pain-related dysfunctional beliefs about sleep and depressive symptoms mediate the influence of pain severity on fear of progression among individuals with cancer.

papers.title: Spatial sampling for triaxial OPM-MEG: understanding neurodevelopmental trajectory.
papers.abstract: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures magnetic fields generated by current flow in neural assemblies, providing a non-invasive means to track brain function. In recent years, the MEG field has been revolutionised by a new class of field sensor called an Optically Pumped Magnetometer (OPM). OPMs are small, lightweight, and allow construction of wearable and reconfigurable arrays of 'triaxial' field sensors (that measure magnetic fields along three axes simultaneously). These systems can be used to capture MEG data across the life span, from infancy to adulthood. With such multi-axis sensing arrays coming into routine use, here we aimed determine how dense a sensor array is required to adequately capture the spatial variation of neuromagnetic fields across the scalp.Approach: We simulated neuromagnetic fields based on realistic head geometries of individuals aged 15 months to 34 years. We then used two independent approaches to determine the sensor spacing required to capture the highest spatial variation of the field across the scalp surface: one method was based on spherical harmonic decomposition of neuromagnetic fields, and the other based on evaluating sensor redundancy in densely sampled arrays.Main results: Both methods agree in showing that the required sensor separation increases with age, from ~40 mm in a 1-year-old to ~55 mm in an adult.Significance: The sensor spacings obtained in our simulations represent upper bounds in the required values: separations above these bounds will not adequately capture spatial field variation; however, continuing to reduce sensor separation below these limits will continue to improve performance. These findings are important for the future development of OPM-MEG technology, particularly the construction of systems for neurodevelopmental applications.

papers.title: Antibody-mediated encephalitides: distinct diseases with transdisciplinary implications.
papers.abstract: The discovery of antibody-mediated glial and neuronal disorders has transformed the diagnosis and treatment of neurological diseases previously considered idiopathic or not recognised as immune-mediated. Antibody-mediated disorders targeting glial aquaporin-4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein are distinct nosological entities, defined by specific targets, mechanisms, syndromes, and therapeutic implications. By contrast, antibody-mediated disorders targeting neuronal antigens (ie, autoimmune encephalitides) are still frequently analysed collectively, with data from different disorders pooled as if they represent a single disease rather than distinct entities. Evidence from anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis, anti-LGI1 encephalitis, and anti-IgLON5 disease (used here as exemplars of autoimmune encephalitides) indicates that individual autoimmune encephalitides differ in demographics, triggers, mechanisms, clinical manifestations, post-acute trajectories, and treatment requirements. The broad, heterogeneous presentations of autoimmune encephalitides require coordinated multidisciplinary care within and beyond neurology, involving specialists in paediatrics, infectious diseases, epilepsy, movement disorders, sleep medicine, intensive care, cognitive rehabilitation, and other relevant disciplines. Such interdisciplinary collaboration facilitates the recognition of new diseases and elucidation of the causes of previously unclassified disorders. Improving patient care requires not only aetiological and mechanistic insight to enable development of targeted therapies but also strengthened cross-specialty expertise to optimise diagnosis and management.

papers.title: Feasibility of implementing a mindfulness-based program for paediatric intensive care unit staff.
papers.abstract: Paediatric intensive care unit (PICU) clinicians are particularly susceptible to workplace stress due to frequent ethical dilemmas (for example, perceptions of futile or unethical treatment), patient morbidity and mortality, sleep disruption, and emotional exhaustion, putting them at increased risk of anxiety, depression, and burnout. The psychological well-being of these healthcare professionals is vital for maintaining high standards of patient care and safety. The aim of this study was to evaluate the feasibility of implementing a mindfulness-based program among PICU staff, with a focus on acceptability and barriers to participation. Weekly 20-min guided group-practice sessions in mindfulness, with both in-person and virtual attendance options, were held over a 6-month period. These sessions were offered to medical, nursing, and allied health staff working in the PICU of a specialist paediatric hospital in Queensland, Australia, serving families from Queensland and northern New South Wales. The program was offered during a period of increased personal and occupational stress arising from the delivery of high-acuity care during the global COVID-19 pandemic. The program was successfully delivered within the PICU setting, with most participants expressing interest in continuation of the program (72%). Qualitative responses suggested perceived individual and collective well-being benefits, alongside generally positive perceptions of the program. However, participants also identified important barriers to participation, including workload pressures and rostering constraints. This study suggests that implementation of a mindfulness-based program within a PICU setting may be feasible while also highlighting important operational barriers to participation in high-acuity healthcare environments. Qualitative findings indicated generally positive staff perceptions and perceived acceptability of the program. Further research using longitudinal designs is recommended to better understand implementation considerations and potential longer-term outcomes associated with mindfulness-based interventions in PICU settings.
papers.journal: Australian critical care : official journal of the Confederation of Australian Critical Care Nurses

papers.title: In-laboratory polysomnography as the reference standard in sleep research: a bibliometric overview of human studies.
papers.abstract: In-laboratory attended Polysomnography (PSG) is the reference standard for objective sleep assessment. Although portable and wearable sleep technologies have advanced, the evolution of PSG research over the past decade has not been systematically characterized. Bibliometric data from the Web of Science Core Collection (2015-2025) were retrieved using a search strategy focused on in-laboratory, full-night PSG studies, yielding 462 publications for analysis. VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and Microsoft Excel were used to conduct visual and quantitative analyses of publication trends, country- and institution-level co-authorship, journal distribution, author keywords, and keywords bursts. Annual publications exhibited a steady increase, with the United States and China as the leading contributors. Prominent institutions included Eindhoven University of Technology and Seoul National University. PSG research was predominantly published in specialized sleep medicine journals. Keyword analysis revealed a stable thematic core encompassing sleep monitoring, sleep staging, and sleep apnea, alongside emerging trends in machine learning, wearable devices, and brain modeling. Within the corpus of included in-laboratory PSG studies, research outputs demonstrated a sustained trajectory, exhibiting a pattern of parallel development between clinical applications and technical refinement. While PSG remains a foundational methodological pillar in this specific domain, its evolving integration with advanced computational methods underscores a continued commitment to bridging clinical relevance and technological progress within PSG-focused research.

papers.title: Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: a critical narrative review of modern concepts and unani perspectives.
papers.abstract: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a chronic, disabling, multisystem illness characterized by persistent fatigue, post-exertional malaise/post-exertional symptom exacerbation (PEM/PESE), unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive impairment. Classical Unani medicine does not recognize ME/CFS as a distinct disease entity. However, its descriptions of fatigue (I'yā), particularly I'yā Dhātī (spontaneous fatigue), provide a basis for examining parallels with ME/CFS. To examine I'yā Dhātī (spontaneous fatigue) and its three simple subtypes (I'yā Qarūḥī, I'yā Tamaddudī, and I'yā Waramī) and compare them qualitatively with contemporary ME/CFS, including areas of similarity and discordance. This critical narrative review used structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science. Eight primary Unani sources were examined: Al-Qānūn fi al-Ṭibb, Kulliyāt al-Qānūn, Kitāb al-Ḥāwī, Kitāb al-Murshid, Kitāb al-Manṣūrī, Dhakhīrah-i Khwārazm Shāhī, Kitāb al-Kulliyāt, and Al-Mukhtārāt fi al-Ṭibb. The three subtypes were compared using predefined qualitative domains based on contemporary ME/CFS features and classical descriptions. I'yā Tamaddudī (distensive fatigue) showed the greatest phenomenological overlap with ME/CFS, particularly spontaneous fatigue, generalized heaviness, sleep disturbances, mental dullness, reduced functional capacity, and diffuse somatic manifestations. However, no clearly documented classical equivalent of delayed PEM/PESE was identified, representing a major area of discordance. I'yā Tamaddudī (distensive fatigue) showed the greatest phenomenological/conceptual overlap with ME/CFS among the subtypes examined. This represents a historical and interpretative correspondence, not biological, diagnostic, or therapeutic equivalence. Independent operationalization and prospective evaluation are required before its clinical or biological relevance can be established.

papers.title: Solriamfetol for residual sleepiness and its impact on continuous positive airway pressure adherence: A French database analysis.
papers.abstract: Solriamfetol may improve obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome (OSA) while potentially influencing CPAP adherence. To investigate the impact of solriamfetol initiation for residual sleepiness on CPAP adherence and termination rates in adults with OSA. Data from the French Système National des Données de Santé (SNDS) database, which contains data on health spending reimbursements for > 99% of all individuals living in France, were analyzed. All OSA patients who received at least one administration of solriamfetol for between 09/01/2021 and 06/30/2023 and who received at least one CPAP reimbursement in the 12 months before the index date of solriamfetol administration were included. A CPAP adherence score was calculated based on the reimbursement levels for this treatment over 4-week periods: score = 3 (more than 4 hours per night on average), score = 2 (between 2 and 4 hours per night on average), score = 1 (less than 2 hours per night on average), patient no longer using CPAP: score=0. For each patient, we calculated the average score over 6 sequences of 4 weeks preceding and following the index date of solriamfetol initiation. A control group from the SNDS CPAP-treated OSA was matched by propensity score to subjects treated with CPAP and solriamfetol. 930 OSA patients initiated on solriamfetol were included and matched to 8,920 controls. The characteristics of the cases and controls were similar (age = 56.4 and 57.1 years, 64.5% and 64.6% male, and same burden of comorbidities). During the 6 months before and after the start of solriamfetol treatment, the mean CPAP adherence score was slightly but significantly higher in the solriamfetol group than in the control group (before: 2.8 vs. 2.6, p < 0.0001, after: 2.8 vs. 2.5, p < 0.0001). We found no evidence that solriamfetol initiation was associated with reduced CPAP adherence.

papers.title: Exploring infant safe sleep practices and sleep arrangement motivations in a South African sample.
papers.abstract: Sudden unexpected infant death remains a significant public health concern, with South Africa reporting among the highest incidence globally. However, little is known about infant sleep practices, motivations for sleep arrangements, or adherence to safe sleep recommendations within this context. This study explored caregiver and child characteristics associated with potential sleep-related risk, and caregiver motivations underlying infant sleep arrangements, among South African caregivers. A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 201 caregivers of infants. Prevalence of adherence to American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines was determined. A safe sleep composite score, derived from items of the Brief Infant Sleep Questionnaire-Revised, classified caregivers into low-, moderate-, and high-adherence groups. Bivariate associations between demographic characteristics and low-adherence group membership were examined using chi-square tests, with hierarchical multiple regression to identify predictors of adherence to guidelines. Prevalence of motivations for sleep arrangements were determined and compared across demographic characteristics. Bed-sharing and non-supine sleeping was common. Unemployed caregivers were more than twice as likely to fall into the low-adherence group (45.9% vs. 20.5%), and caregiver characteristics explained significant variance beyond child characteristics (ΔR2 = 0.20, p = .022), with unemployment the only significant independent predictor. No child characteristics were associated with adherence. Feeding, bonding, and safety were the primary motivations for bed and room-sharing, while separate-room sleeping motivations centered on caregiver sleep quality. Adherence to guidelines is complex. Caregiver characteristics were associated with potential sleep-related risk. Findings support safe sleep interventions tailored to caregivers' practical and socioeconomic circumstances, particularly for unemployed and single caregivers.

papers.title: Circadian rhythm maturation in infancy: a large-scale analysis of sleep-wake pattern development from 3 to 18 months based on longitudinal data.
papers.abstract: Infant sleep-wake rhythms consolidate rapidly during the first year, yet normative trajectories and their variability remain poorly characterized. We examined sleep-wake development between 3 and 18 months using prospective, event-level data from a large international cohort. Sleep logs from 175,593 infants (10.7 million logged days) were collected via a mobile tracking application. Parents recorded each sleep event prospectively. We analyzed developmental changes in daytime sleep and nap frequency, compensation during nap transitions, bedtime stability as a circadian marker, relationships between sleep timing and need, and rank-order stability of individual differences. Total sleep decreased from 14.8 h at 3 months to 12.5 h at 18 months, reflected almost entirely by reductions in daytime sleep (226 to 101 min) as nap frequency declined from 3.9 to 1.0 per day. During the early nap transitions, the remaining naps lengthened to compensate for 88-89% of the sleep time lost when a nap was dropped. Compensation was lower during the transition from two naps to one nap (79%). Within-infant bedtime variability decreased most steeply before 9 months, consistent with circadian consolidation. Individual differences in bedtime regularity were highly stable across age periods (Spearman r = 0.73-0.77). Infants with greater sleep need had earlier bedtimes and more daytime sleep, while daytime sleep and time in bed were negatively correlated (r = -0.48). The decline in total sleep across infancy results from reductions in daytime sleep through fewer and eventually shorter naps. Bedtime regularity increases most rapidly before 9 months, and individual differences emerge early and persist, suggesting enduring circadian traits are already established in infancy. Substantial inter-individual variability underscores the importance of individually tailored guidance.

papers.title: CNPY3 variants associated with a recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathy affect inflammasome and TLR function.
papers.abstract: Canopy FGF signalling regulator 3 (CNPY3) is an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident chaperone essential for toll-like receptor (TLR) folding, trafficking and inflammasome activation. In rare paediatric cases, biallelic CNPY3 variants have been associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), but available data remain sparse. 50 individuals from 38 unrelated families with biallelic CNPY3 variants and DEE were evaluated for exome and genome findings, standardised clinical phenotype descriptions, EEG results, and neuroimaging data. A selection of variants underwent functional analysis focussing on protein stability and localisation, TLR2 function, NLPR3 inflammasome activation, and structural conformation. Disease onset occurred in early infancy (median age at onset 68 days), with a clinical phenotype comprising global developmental delay (100%) and intractable epilepsy (86%), accompanied by microcephaly (70%), spasticity (77%), growth faltering (63%), stridor (48%), and early mortality (38%). Epileptic spasms and tonic seizures (46% each) were the most frequent seizure types, and EEG findings included suppression-burst (37%) and hypsarrhythmia (28%). Phenotypic severity varied substantially, with most patients being severely affected (median score 16, range 2-20). Most variants occurred in the homozygous state (95%), including 13 missense changes and 7 truncating alleles. Variants were classified as of uncertain significance (71%), followed by likely pathogenic (23%) and pathogenic (6%) according to ACMG/AMP criteria. Genotype-phenotype correlation showed that individuals with truncating variants were, on average, more severely affected than those with non-truncating variants (median score 18 vs 14.5). Protein modelling predicted conformational effects for most missense variants. In cells, frameshift alleles abolished CNPY3 protein expression, whereas nonsense alleles markedly reduced protein levels. ER localisation of CNPY3 remained preserved across tested genotypes; however, capacity to support TLR2 maturation and processing varied substantially. Remarkably, some missense variants permitted TLR2 surface expression but impaired downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, uncoupling trafficking from signal transduction. CNPY3-associated DEE is a severe early-onset disorder with genotype-dependent phenotypic severity, accompanied by allele-specific disruption of innate immune pathways. Our findings reveal separable effects on TLR trafficking, downstream signalling and inflammasome activation, identifying CNPY3 as a key regulator of multiple cellular pathways involved in inflammatory responses and neurodevelopment. papers.title: A scoping literature review of factors associated with burnout among student pharmacists in the United States.
papers.abstract: Burnout is an increasing challenge among student pharmacists. Individual studies have examined burnout among student pharmacists; however, faculty and college administrators lack a consolidated understanding of the educational, personal, and contextual factors associated with burnout. This scoping literature review explored factors associated with burnout among student pharmacists in the United States. For this scoping literature review, MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, and PsycINFO were searched for English-language studies published between January 2000 and February 2026. Records were deduplicated in EndNote and Covidence. Eligible studies reported factors associated with burnout or related outcomes, including emotional exhaustion, anxiety, depression, and poor well-being. Quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods studies were included. Two independent reviewers screened studies, assessed full texts, and extracted data, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Reporting followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Eleven studies met the inclusion criteria from 2893 screened records. Most were published since 2020, used observational survey designs, and included students from one or more United States colleges of pharmacy. Validated burnout measures, primarily the Maslach Burnout Inventory and Oldenburg Burnout Inventory, were commonly used. Burnout was associated with intrinsic program factors (year in program, workload, competitive culture, campus assignment), extrinsic factors (co-curricular activities, employment, career planning), and individual factors (sex, marital status, sleep, nutrition, resilience, lack of time). One randomized trial found a mindfulness application reduced burnout after six weeks, although longer-term effects were mixed. Burnout requires systemic curricular reform, integrated wellness initiatives, and longitudinal, multi-institutional research to improve student well-being and reduce burnout.

papers.title: ReBAN-Net: An interpretable hybrid deep learning framework for ECG-based emotion recognition.
papers.abstract: Emotional assessment is essential for mental health management, yet questionnaire-based scales are subjective and facial- or voice-based approaches can be influenced by intentional behavior and environmental interference. This study proposes ReBAN-Net, a hybrid architecture integrating a one-dimensional residual convolutional network, a bidirectional long short-term memory network, and a soft attention mechanism for ECG-based emotion recognition. Three classification tasks were defined throughout the study: nine-class valence classification (levels 1-9), nine-class arousal classification (levels 1-9), and four-class affective-state classification (baseline, stress, amusement, and meditation). The model was evaluated on the WESAD dataset using a strict 15-fold leave-one-subject-out protocol. It achieved accuracies of 86.03% for nine-class valence, 86.27% for nine-class arousal, and 87.58% for four-class affective-state classification, with corresponding macro-AUC values of 96.07%, 96.24%, and 95.09%. Temporal class activation and attention-feature analyses show that the model focuses on physiologically meaningful ECG regions. These results demonstrate the feasibility and interpretability of ReBAN-Net and indicate its potential for subject-independent ECG-based emotion recognition.

papers.title: Adult Attention Deficit-Hyperactivity Disorder.
papers.abstract: Attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a medical condition that is present in approximately 2.5% of adults worldwide and manifests in a variety of different ways across the lifespan. Adults with ADHD often have coexisting psychiatric disorders such as anxiety, mood, sleep, substance use, and personality disorders and are at increased risk for coexisting somatic conditions such as obesity, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, and immune and inflammatory conditions. Hence, such adults may be seen by clinicians providing care for a wide range of psychiatric and somatic conditions. Nevertheless, ADHD remains unrecognized and undiagnosed in many persons. Assessment requires interviewing of the patient for core ADHD symptoms, coexisting conditions, and their functional effects, which can be facilitated by using standardized rating scales. Key components of treatment are psychoeducation and psychostimulant or nonstimulant medication, mostly in combination with psychosocial interventions and lifestyle guidance.
papers.journal: The New England journal of medicine

papers.title: Passive Language Mapping With High-Gamma Modulations.
papers.abstract: Passive language mapping using high-gamma modulation (HGM) has emerged as a valuable tool in both presurgical evaluation for epilepsy and neuroscientific discovery. HGM mapping leverages task-related synchronization in high-gamma frequencies to identify language areas without the risks associated with electrical stimulation mapping. This review outlines the principles and techniques used in the field of HGM-based mapping, including electrode types, referencing schemes, power analysis, and localization techniques. We survey a range of cognitive tasks-speech production, auditory processing, reading, and memory-that elicit language-related HGM responses and discuss their relevance to comprehensive language mapping. We examine perspectives on methodologic challenges, including artifact management, variability across patients, and spatial sampling. We assess validation studies comparing HGM with electrical stimulation mapping and neuropsychological outcomes, noting HGM's unique role in identifying language cortex in pediatric and cognitively impaired populations. Finally, we speculate on the future directions of the field, including integration with corticocortical evoked potentials and the potential for HGM-informed speech synthesis. As the field matures, HGM mapping is poised to contribute to improved clinical outcomes and enhance our understanding of the dynamics and development of the human language network.
