papers.title: Characterization of the Bispectral Index in Healthy Volunteers Receiving Inhalation Anesthetics in Combination With Opioids in a Randomized Trial.
papers.abstract: Processed electroencephalogram (pEEG) monitors are commonly used in anesthesia practice. The relationship between the pEEG and clinical levels of sedation over anesthetic concentrations with and without opioids is not well understood. The purpose of this trial was to investigate the relationship between Bispectral IndexTM (BISTM), clinical measures of sedation, and inhaled anesthetics across a range of anesthetic concentrations and hypnotic states with and without intravenous opioids. This prospective, randomized trial enrolled 211 healthy volunteers. Participants were randomized to one of five anesthetic regimens: sevoflurane, sevoflurane with remifentanil, sevoflurane with fentanyl, desflurane, or isoflurane. Target anesthetic end-tidal concentrations were increased in a stepwise fashion until a BIS index of 30 to 40 was reached. Opioids were administered by target-controlled infusion and commenced before the inhaled agent began. At each targeted end-tidal concentration, responsiveness was assessed using the Modified Observer's Assessment of Alertness/Sedation (MOAA/S) score and the BIS index was recorded. The MOAA/S score was used to assess participant responsiveness, with a score ≤2 considered unresponsive and a score ≥3 considered responsive. The primary outcome measure was the BIS50 for each anesthetic regimen, representing the BIS index at which 50% of participants were unresponsive. Secondary outcomes included BIS95 (representing the BIS index at which 95% of participants were unresponsive) and evaluation of the BIS index as a predictor of responsiveness. BIS50 and BIS95 were estimated using random intercept logistic regression models, and the predictive performance of BIS indices was assessed by calculating the corresponding area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). One hundred and forty-three participants were randomized to a treatment group and completed the procedure with adequate data. Mean age was 26.5 ± 6.7 years (52% male). There were no reported device-related adverse events. Across treatment groups, BIS50 ranged from 67.5 (95% confidence interval [CI], 63.6-71.4) to 76.2 (73.5-78.8), and BIS95 ranged from 49.1 (42.9-55.4) to 63.3 (59.5-67.2). Compared to the sevoflurane and isoflurane groups, the desflurane group exhibited slightly lower BIS50 and BIS95 values. The addition of opioids to sevoflurane had minimal impact on BIS50 and BIS95. The BIS index alone was a strong predictor of the level of responsiveness, with AUCs consistently close to the ideal value of 1 (≥0.95) across all treatment groups. BIS indices were highly correlated with MOAA/S scores. These results describe the relationship between BIS levels and responsiveness for commonly used volatile anesthetics, with and without opioids, across a range of anesthetic concentrations. The results of this study should be interpreted in light of the study design which included young, healthy adult volunteers with no sustained, noxious stimulation. These findings may not be generalizable to other populations or clinical situations.

papers.title: Open-Loop Deep Brain Stimulation Versus Closed-Loop Responsive Neurostimulation in Drug-Resistant Bitemporal Epilepsy: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Drug-resistant bitemporal epilepsy presents a therapeutic challenge when resective surgery is not feasible due to bilateral seizure onset or eloquent cortex involvement. Neuromodulation has emerged as an alternative, with open-loop deep brain stimulation (DBS) and closed-loop responsive neurostimulation (RNS) as implantable strategies. Comparative indications for modality selection remain unclear. A narrative review of articles published from January 2007 to January 2026 was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE. Approximately 120 articles were screened, and 39 studies were included. Due to heterogeneity in study design, findings were synthesized qualitatively. Both DBS and RNS significantly reduce seizure frequency in drug-resistant bitemporal epilepsy, with a median seizure reduction of approximately 60% to 75%. Seizure freedom, however, remained limited, reflecting the palliative nature of these treatments. Open-loop anterior nucleus of the thalamus (ANT) DBS provides network-level modulation with low maintenance, while hippocampal DBS offers localized temporal inhibition. Conversely, closed-loop RNS delivers adaptive focal stimulation via real-time sensing and yields chronic intracranial electroencephalogram data. While both modalities show comparable efficacy, RNS may be advantageous in focal or asymmetric bitemporal epilepsy. Cognitive outcomes were favorable for both techniques, with RNS demonstrating the prevention of memory and language decline. Both DBS and RNS are palliative neuromodulatory options for patients in whom resective surgery is not feasible. Treatment selection should be individualized based on seizure network characteristics, laterality, monitoring needs, participation capacity, and cognitive considerations. The primary goal is to reduce seizure frequency and improve quality of life rather than to achieve seizure freedom. Future multicenter studies and biomarker-driven strategies are needed to refine selection and improve long-term outcomes.
papers.journal: Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology

papers.title: TIME FOR COFFEE coordinates phase separation and chromatin regulation for salt tolerance.
papers.abstract: The circadian clock enhances plant fitness by aligning internal timing with the external photoperiod, but how it coordinates spatiotemporal regulation with chromatin dynamics to improve salt tolerance is not well understood. Here, we show that the clock component TIME FOR COFFEE (TIC) forms biomolecular condensates in response to salt stress, but not to osmotic stress alone. Consistently, tic mutants were hypersensitive to salt stress yet displayed enhanced salt tolerance under 21-hour light-dark cycles matching their shortened circadian period, highlighting the importance of circadian clock in salt tolerance. Salt stress increases H3K9ac levels at the salt stress-responsive genes and induces their expression in a time-of-day-dependent manner in wild-type plants, whereas both H3K9ac level and transcriptional activation are attenuated in tic mutants. TIC physically associates with HD2-type histone deacetylases, and a subset of HD2 partially colocalizes with TIC condensates in the nucleolus under salt stress. Genetic and biochemical analyses showed that salt stress promotes TIC condensate formation, accompanied by reduced HD2 occupancy at salt stress-responsive loci, thereby elevating H3K9ac levels and promoting gene expression. Together, these findings uncover a mechanism by which salt-induced TIC condensate formation links chromatin regulation with circadian timing, thereby promoting plant adaptation to salt stress.

papers.title: Short-term subjective and EEG responses following cervical rotatory manipulation are not reproduced by simulated cracking sound: A randomized controlled study.
papers.abstract: Cervical rotatory manipulation (CRM) is commonly used for neck-related symptoms and is often accompanied by a cracking sound. Whether a simulated cracking sound can reproduce the short-term subjective and neurophysiological responses to the complete CRM remains unclear. This study compared short-term subjective and electroencephalography (EEG) responses to CRM with those following sham manipulation with or without a simulated cracking sound. In this randomized controlled trial with three parallel groups and a single intervention session, 54 healthy volunteers were allocated to CRM, sham manipulation, or sham + simulated sound. Positive affect, negative affect, comfort, satisfaction, and eyes closed resting state EEG were assessed before and after the intervention. Prespecified EEG derived outcomes included frontal alpha power, frontal alpha/beta ratio, occipital individual alpha frequency, and alpha band frontoparietal and frontotemporal functional connectivity. CRM produced greater improvements in positive affect, comfort, and satisfaction than sham manipulation or sham + simulated cracking sound, whereas no clear difference among groups was observed for negative affect. Differences among groups were also observed in frontal alpha/beta ratio and alpha band frontoparietal and frontotemporal functional connectivity. Sham + simulated sound did not reproduce the overall pattern of subjective and EEG responses observed after CRM. CRM produced greater improvements over the short-term in positive affect, comfort, and satisfaction and was accompanied by differences in selected resting state EEG outcomes compared with sham manipulation with or without simulated cracking sound. Adding simulated cracking sound to sham manipulation did not reproduce this pattern. Because CRM differed from the control conditions in several procedural components, the specific component or combination of components responsible for these differences could not be determined. The trial was registered with the International Traditional Medicine Clinical Trial Registry (URL: https://itmctr.ccebtcm.org.cn; ITMCTR2025001112).

papers.title: Disrupted fear regulation in insomnia disorder revealed by arousal estimation from skin conductance.
papers.abstract: Insomnia disorder (ID) is a common sleep-wake disorder marked by persistent dissatisfaction with sleep quality or quantity. Previous studies have shown that sleep plays a critical role in emotion regulation, particularly in fear extinction. This study aims to characterize ID using estimates of the sympathetic arousal state derived from skin conductance (SC)-based observations, and to compare two observation models: the marked point process (MPP) model and the MPP coupled with continuous (MPP+Cont) model. We utilize SC data from a fear conditioning and extinction procedure involving 24 individuals with ID and 24 good sleepers (GS). The SC measurements are deconvolved to extract autonomic nervous system (ANS) activations and the tonic component. The MPP observation model uses only the extracted ANS activations, while the MPP+Cont model incorporates both ANS activations and the tonic component. Both models are employed to estimate the underlying arousal state over time and compute a high arousal index (HAI). We compare the estimated arousal states and HAI between the ID and GS groups to assess alterations in arousal associated with ID. Our results reveal that ID may be associated with impaired fear extinction learning and recall. Notably, the distinction between ID and GS emerges only under the MPP+Cont model, indicating the critical role of the tonic component in arousal estimation. Overall, this study highlights the potential of arousal state estimation for understanding autonomic dysregulation in ID, thereby supporting interventions for fear-centered comorbidities and improving quality of life.

papers.title: Investigating the transfer of physical stimuli to the dreamed body: A comparative study of muscular, vestibular, and haptic stimulation on dream incorporation.
papers.abstract: The relationship between the dreamed body and the physical body remains an open question in sleep and dream research. This study examined whether somatosensory stimulation applied during REM sleep modulates the corresponding dream content under controlled conditions. Using a within-subject design, we compared three stimulation modalities-electrical muscular, galvanic vestibular, and haptic vibration-each paired with a modality-specific sham stimulation. Twenty-four participants completed one adaptation night followed by three consecutive experimental nights in the sleep laboratory. Dream reports were collected following rapid eye movement sleep awakenings after stimulation or sham periods, yielding a total of 120 reports. Dream incorporation of bodily sensations and actions was observed across all conditions; however, generalized linear mixed-effects analyses revealed no statistically significant differences between stimulation and sham conditions for any modality. No evidence for reliable modality-specific dream incorporation was observed under rigorous sham-controlled conditions. Rather than demonstrating robust stimulation-specific effects, these findings suggest that contextual and expectancy-related influences substantially contribute to bodily dream content under laboratory conditions while highlighting methodological challenges in dream incorporation research. By combining multiple somatosensory stimulation modalities with rigorous sham-controlled procedures, the present study provides a methodological benchmark for future investigations of dream incorporation and dream engineering.

papers.title: Multifactorial explanatory model of self-reported sleep disturbance in people with rheumatoid arthritis: a structural equation approach.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbance is a common and disabling symptom among patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). This study aimed to test a multifactorial explanatory model of cross-sectional associations among factors related to self-reported sleep disturbance in RA. This was an ancillary analysis of an observational, cross-sectional, single-centre study including patients with RA. Sleep disturbance, disease activity, perceived disease impact, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and personality traits were assessed using validated questionnaires. Structural equation modelling (SEM) was used to examine the associations between sleep disturbance and the remaining variables. A total of 313 patients (82% female; mean age 60±12 years; disease duration 12±9 years) were included. The final model showed an acceptable fit to the data [χ2(71)=178.04, χ2/df=2.50, p<0.005; CFI=0.95; GFI=0.92; TLI=0.94; RMSEA=0.07, p=0.004, 95% CI=0.06 to 0.08] and explained 57% of the variance of self-reported sleep disturbance (R2=0.57). Disease activity was positively associated with disease impact (β=0.23; p<0.001), which was significantly associated with sleep disturbance (β=0.65; p=0.001). 'Positive' personality traits were inversely associated with self-reported sleep disturbance (β= -0.51; p=0.001), with direct (β= -0.16; p=0.006) and indirect associations (β= -0.35; p=0.001) through perceived disease impact. They were also inversely associated with depression (β= -0.77; p=0.001) and anxiety (β= -0.80; p<0.001). Depression and anxiety were positively associated with perceived disease impact (β=0.38; p=0.001 and β=0.30; p<0.001, respectively). 'Positive' personality traits and perceived disease impact appear to be significantly associated with self-reported sleep disturbance in RA patients, while disease activity, depression, and anxiety showed comparatively smaller associations within the model. These findings support the need for a holistic, multidisciplinary approach to RA management.

papers.title: Nonlinear associations between sleep duration and psychological frailty in an aging Chinese population: insights from a national cohort.
papers.abstract: To examine the longitudinal and nonlinear association between sleep duration and psychological frailty in middle-aged and older Chinese adults. We analyzed 9,476 participants aged ≥45 years in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. leep duration was reported in 2011, and psychological frailty was assessed using thePsychological Frailty Index in 2018. We examined associations using multivariable logistic regression and restricted cubic splines. Sensitivity analyses incorporated sleep measurements from 2013 and 2015, three-wave average sleep duration, sleep trajectories, and multiple imputation. Short nighttime sleep (<6 h) was associated with higher odds of psychological frailty compared with 6-8 h of sleep (OR = 1.27, 95% CI: 1.08-1.51, p = 0.005). We observed nonlinear associations, with estimated turning points at 7.56 h for nighttime sleep and 8.55 h for total sleep. Persistent short sleep was also associated with higher odds of psychological frailty (OR = 1.44, 95% CI: 1.15-1.81, p = 0.002). Multiple-imputation analyses yielded broadly similar estimates. Short nighttime sleep and persistent short sleep were associated with psychological frailty in middle-aged and older Chinese adults. These findings suggest that sleep duration may be relevant to psychological health although causal relationships remain to be established.

papers.title: Affective symptoms in focal epilepsy: A scoping review of localization and lateralizing findings.
papers.abstract: Emotional experiences during focal seizures are often misinterpreted as psychiatric disorders. We aimed to evaluate symptoms involving affective symptoms at seizure onset. We aimed to identify the most prevalent affective symptoms at seizure onset and characterize their localizing and lateralizing value. We performed a scoping review based on Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses-extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. A systematic search identified records from 4 databases: PubMed, Embase, CINAHL (via EBSCOhost), and Web of Science. Two reviewers independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts; discrepancies were resolved by consensus. This review focused on patients with focal seizures, as affective symptoms may occur in generalized epilepsies. The affective symptoms: fear, anxiety, panic, sadness, mystic, ecstatic, sexual, and mirth were identified, and semiology was evaluated in accordance with ILAE guidelines. Symptom onset, frequency, brain localization, and video-EEG monitoring technique were evaluated to assess localization and lateralization of regional networks. Scalp EEG, invasive EEG recordings, and electrical stimulation were analyzed. A total of 1276 documents were identified, with 98 studies included for review. Fear was the most frequently reported ictal emotion, identified in 274 patients (66%), predominantly in temporal lobe epilepsy. Sadness and sexual, ecstatic symptoms were also consistently associated with temporal networks. Mirth was more frequently reported with frontal onset seizures. Evidence, primarily from Class IV studies, reported right hemispheric predominance for ecstasy, mystic, and sexual symptoms at seizure onset. Ictal affective symptoms at seizure onset yield localizing information. The limbic system, especially the temporal lobe, followed by the frontal lobe, was the most common site of origin. Fear was the most common spontaneous and electrically elicited symptom, followed by anxiety. While bi-hemispheric lateralization occurred, right lateralization predominated. Recognizing paroxysmal affective symptoms as ictal phenomena may reduce misdiagnosis and aid presurgical evaluation in drug-resistant focal epilepsy.
papers.journal: Epileptic disorders : international epilepsy journal with videotape

papers.title: Pharmacological and Nonpharmacological Interventions to Address Insomnia Symptoms and Poor Sleep Quality Among People With HIV: Protocol for a Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: HIV-related research has increasingly focused on addressing long-term comorbidities affecting health-related quality of life for people with HIV. Sleep-related conditions, such as insomnia, are highly prevalent among people with HIV and are associated with a variety of health challenges, including immune dysregulation, increased mental health burden, and reduced antiretroviral therapy adherence. Although there are several evidence-based pharmacological (eg, hypnotics) and nonpharmacological interventions (eg, cognitive behavioral therapy) to treat insomnia, few have been specifically tested among people with HIV. The objective of this scoping review is to characterize the current state of the field regarding pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions for treating insomnia symptoms and poor sleep quality among adults (aged 18 years or older) with HIV. Eligible studies are those that (1) are focused on adults with HIV (aged ≥18 years), (2) examine the effects of an intervention (pharmacological or nonpharmacological) within this population, and (3) have a primary outcome dedicated to sleep quality and/or insomnia symptoms. All published manuscripts, abstracts, conference proceedings, and currently registered studies in the clinical trials registry will be considered. The review will follow the JBI scoping review methodology and adhere to the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) reporting standards. A comprehensive literature search will be conducted by searching MEDLINE, Embase, PsycInfo, CINAHL, Web of Science Core Collection, Cochrane CENTRAL, and ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global databases in July 2026. Two reviewers will independently screen abstracts and titles using Covidence, with a third reviewer resolving any conflicts via consensus meetings. Full-text reviews of selected studies will then be conducted to determine final study eligibility. Data from included studies will then be independently extracted using a pilot-tested extraction form that captures participant characteristics, study details, intervention design, and sleep-related outcomes. A thorough narrative review with a summary table of study characteristics and findings will be generated at the end of the scoping review process. The scoping review process began in April 2026. The authors anticipate identifying relevant full-text articles by December 2026 and completing the initial review of all eligible manuscripts by January 2027. Final results are expected to be consolidated and submitted for publication in the spring or summer of 2027. The results of this scoping review will help to contextualize the current landscape of potentially helpful interventions to improve insomnia symptoms and poor sleep quality among people with HIV through an updated, more comprehensive review of the literature. Understanding the types of pharmacological and nonpharmacological interventions to treat insomnia symptoms and poor sleep that have already been tested among people with HIV may provide targeted guidance for optimizing personalized behavioral and medical treatments to improve sleep health in this underserved population.

papers.title: Acute Delirium Management in Hospice and Palliative Care.
papers.abstract: Acute delirium is a serious neurocognitive disorder that is highly prevalent among individuals receiving hospice and palliative care. Delirium causes significant distress for patients, families, and healthcare providers while contributing to prolonged hospitalization, increased healthcare utilization and costs, a greater likelihood of institutionalization, shorter survival, and higher mortality. It is characterized by acute disturbances in attention and awareness that often fluctuate throughout the day and may present as hypoactive, hyperactive, or mixed psychomotor subtypes. Delirium can be challenging to identify because of its overlapping features with other neurocognitive disorders, such as dementia. Routine screening using validated assessment tools is essential for early identification and treatment. Effective prevention and management of delirium require a multifaceted, interprofessional approach that addresses modifiable risk factors, as well as the underlying acute medical causes. Hospice and palliative care nurses play a central role in implementing evidence-based nonpharmacological interventions and engaging family care partners to reduce symptom burden and improve outcomes through goal-concordant, supportive strategies, including early mobility, hydration, sleep-wake regulation, and careful pharmacological stewardship.
papers.journal: Journal of hospice and palliative nursing : JHPN : the official journal of the Hospice and Palliative Nurses Association

papers.title: Nonlinear age-related differences in clinical profiles of obstructive sleep apnea: a cross-sectional study of 1,508 Chinese patients.
papers.abstract: To characterize age-related clinical profiles and nonlinear age associations in treatment-naive Chinese patients with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This retrospective cross-sectional study included 1,508 patients aged 18-88 years at Peking Union Medical College Hospital (2022-2025). Clinical and polysomnographic characteristics were compared across five age groups. Restricted cubic splines assessed continuous-age associations, with separate overall and nonlinearity tests and sex-adjusted sensitivity analyses. Sex-adjusted logistic models evaluated prevalent severity, sleepiness, and cardiometabolic comorbidities; age-quartile comparisons were supplementary. Among 1,840 participants undergoing PSG, OSA detection differed across ages, with a greater increase among women (age-by-sex interaction P = 0.031). Respiratory severity was broadly comparable across age groups. In unadjusted analyses, body mass index and Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores showed nonlinear age associations (both P < 0.001), as did lowest oxygen saturation (P = 0.018) and selected Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) components. Global PSQI was associated with age overall, without clear nonlinearity (P = 0.099). Sex adjustment attenuated nonlinearity for oxygen saturation and sleep latency. Older age was associated with higher prevalence odds of hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes. Excessive daytime sleepiness showed a midlife elevation. OSA clinical profiles differ across ages, with nonlinearity in selected measures. Older patients have greater comorbidity burden and poorer reported sleep quality despite comparable respiratory severity.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Microstate Dynamics and their Associations with Acclimatization Index and Serum Albumin in Healthy Adults with Chronic High-Altitude Exposure.
papers.abstract: High-altitude hypoxia has been examined with conventional electroencephalography (EEG), event-related potentials, and neuroimaging, but its association with millisecond-scale resting-state EEG microstate dynamics and peripheral physiology remains unclear. We studied healthy adults including 124 low-altitude (LA) participants (50 men, 74 women) and 174 high-altitude (HA) participants (42 men, 132 women; age 28.05 ± 8.59 years; age unavailable for LA). Coverage, duration, global explained variance (GEV), occurrence, and transition probabilities were extracted for four canonical microstates. LA-HA differences were tested using unadjusted linear models; within-HA associations among the high-altitude acclimatization index (AAI), serum albumin, and Microstate A-related indicators were examined using covariate-adjusted regressions and exploratory bootstrapped mediation analyses. Compared with LA participants, HA participants showed increased Microstate A duration and GEV, decreased occurrence, and unchanged coverage, together with reduced Microstate B-related indicators, enhanced Microstate C-related indicators, and increased A→B and A→C transitions. Within HA participants, AAI was negatively associated with serum albumin, and exploratory mediation analyses indicated indirect associations between AAI and Coverage A, Occurrence A, GEV A, and Microstate A-originating transitions through serum albumin. These findings suggest that chronic high-altitude exposure is associated with resting-state EEG microstate reorganization in healthy adults and that acclimatization-related individual differences may be linked to Microstate A dynamics through serum albumin-related peripheral status.

papers.title: A dynamic triad: why weight trajectory matters in pediatric obesity, sleep apnea, and metabolic risk.
[Early infantile nystagmus from the neuropediatric perspective].
papers.abstract: The differential diagnostic work-up of (early) infantile nystagmus depends largely on the presence of syndromic or neurological abnormalities, in addition to the child's age and ocular findings. In some cases, a careful medical history and physical examination alone are sufficient to establish a diagnosis. Electrophysiology, imaging, molecular genetics and metabolic diagnostics are further essential components of the neuropediatric part of the problem analysis. This paper aims to provide guidance on how to proceed in a way that is as efficient as possible and as gentle as possible on the child.

papers.title: Current perspectives on the pharmacotherapeutic management of insomnia in Veterans.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a highly prevalent sleep disorder among Veterans and frequently co-occurs with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, chronic pain, and substance use disorders. This review synthesizes the current evidence on pharmacological management of insomnia in Veterans with attention to guideline recommendations, veteran-specific safety considerations, and comorbidity-driven prescribing. We discuss the rationale for reducing long-term reliance on benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine receptor agonists (BZRAs) in favor of agents with more favorable long-term risk profiles. Concurrent prescribing of GABAergic hypnotics with opioids is addressed in the context of existing VA Opioid Safety Initiative policy, FDA labeling, and observational overdose data. Off-label agents such as trazodone and quetiapine continue to be widely used despite limited efficacy evidence for insomnia; their use is best reserved for cases in which better-supported options have failed. Contemporary guidance places cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia as first-line treatment, while pharmacotherapy is reserved for patients who do not respond to, cannot access, or decline behavioral treatment. The 2025 VA/DoD guideline suggests several medications when pharmacotherapy is used, including daridorexant, doxepin, eszopiclone, lemborexant, suvorexant, zaleplon, and zolpidem, and recommends against antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, and trazodone for chronic insomnia disorder.

papers.title: Initial Development and Content Validity of an Occupation-Focused Assessment: Occupations in Higher Education Transitions Inventory.
papers.abstract: University students face occupational disruption during post-secondary transitions, yet existing campus screening tools leave occupational challenges largely unassessed. No comprehensive, occupation-focused screening instrument exists for this population. To describe the theoretical development and content validation of the Occupations in Higher Education Transitions Inventory (OHETI), a screening tool assessing university student adaptation across 10 domains of occupation grounded in the Theory of Occupational Adaptation (OA) a five-phase iterative development process was used: (a) initial item generation; (b) preliminary expert review for face validity (N = 3 occupational therapists with expertise in OA theory); (c) tool reconceptualization based on expert feedback; (d) cognitive interviews with undergraduate students for face validity and comprehensibility (N = 10); and (e) formal content validation using a Content Validity Index (CVI) rating procedure with (N = 6) occupational therapy professionals with clinical and academic experience with emerging adult students. Initial item generation yielded 68 items across seven OA constructs. Expert feedback prompted a fundamental restructuring, producing 116 items across 10 occupations, covering aspects of relative mastery: satisfaction, effectiveness, and efficiency. Revision based on student cognitive interviews resulted in 122 items. Formal content validation produced I-CVI scores ranging from 0.667 to 1.0, with S-CVI scores of 0.9516 for clarity and 0.9435 for relevance. Two items were removed, resulting in a final tool of 120 scorable items across 10 occupations. The OHETI demonstrates strong content and face validity as a theoretically grounded, occupation-focused screening tool for university students. Online administration and individualized feedback distinguish it from existing instruments. Psychometric validation is needed before broad implementation.

papers.title: Fatigue in Different Groups of Disaster Responders after the 2024 Noto Peninsula Earthquake: Group-Specific Associations and Priorities for Intervention.
papers.abstract: To compare fatigue in the external supporters and local public officers who responded to the January 1, 2024 Noto Peninsula Earthquake, identify group-specific factors associated with fatigue, and estimate population-level differences under hypothetical scenarios. A repeated-measures observational study was conducted using responder health surveillance data collected between January and March 2024. Generalized estimating equations were used to compare fatigue levels and examine group-specific associations with operational and health-related factors. G-computation was used to estimate model-based population-level differences in fatigue under hypothetical scenarios in which each factor was set to zero. There were 23,865 observations from 7,135 responders. Local public officers reported greater fatigue than external supporters (β = 2.32, 95% CI: 2.22-2.43). The inability to take meals and breaks and unclear command/task structure were associated with greater fatigue in both groups. Sleep disturbance and irritability had stronger associations with fatigue in external supporters. G-computation showed larger model-based population-level differences under the hypothetical scenarios in local public officers, primarily because operational and health-related problems were more prevalent in this group. Operational factors and health problems were associated with fatigue in disaster responders, and the model-based population-level differences under hypothetical scenarios depended on their prevalence. Increasing the number of responders, provision of rest periods, improving command clarity, and monitoring the health of responders may reduce fatigue and improve disaster responses.

papers.title: The interplay between photoperiod and the circadian clock during vegetative growth.
papers.abstract: Photoperiod, the duration of the daily light phase, is a key seasonal signal that shapes vegetative growth in plants. While its role in controlling the transition to flowering has been extensively characterised, the mechanisms through which photoperiod modulates processes such as hypocotyl elongation, leaf expansion, root growth, and carbon allocation during the vegetative phase are only now coming into focus. Understanding these mechanisms is critical, as the vegetative phase establishes the architecture and resources needed for reproduction. Recent work has revealed that plants possess distinct daylength-measurement mechanisms for flowering and vegetative growth, with twilight-length sensing as a complementary mechanism. The circadian clock translates these signals into daily growth rhythms by restricting growth-promoting factors to defined time windows that widen or narrow depending on daylength, contributing to different growth outcomes between short and long photoperiods. Photoperiod further shapes the daily carbon budget, with opposing energy-sensing pathways dynamically adjusting growth to match carbon availability across the day-night cycle. In this review, we examine how photoperiod regulates vegetative growth in Arabidopsis thaliana, from daylength-measurement systems through clock-controlled transcriptional cascades that drive organ elongation and competitive shade avoidance responses, to carbon economy and stress tolerance. We consider how photoperiod modulates responses to temperature extremes, drought, and salinity, and survey emerging evidence from crops and trees. Finally, we discuss chronoculture, propose experimental recommendations, and highlight outstanding questions for the field.

papers.title: Effectiveness of school-based sleep promotion programs for adolescents: a systematic review with meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: The objective of this review is to assess the effectiveness of school-based sleep promotion programs for adolescents on sleep knowledge, sleep hygiene, sleep quality, sleep behavior, sleep efficiency, health-related quality of life, and depressive or anxiety symptoms. Adolescence is a critical period for physical and mental development, during which, quality sleep is essential. However, many adolescents experience sleep deprivation due to factors such as excessive electronic device use, academic and peer pressures, stress, and anxiety. School-based sleep promotion programs have been proposed to address these issues, but their effectiveness remains unclear. This review included studies published in English, Spanish, and Portuguese that assessed the effectiveness of school-based sleep promotion programs for adolescents aged 10 to 19 years on sleep knowledge, sleep hygiene, sleep quality, sleep efficiency, sleep behavior, health-related quality of life, and depressive or anxiety symptoms. Both randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies, with or without a comparator, were eligible. A comprehensive search strategy was used to identify relevant published and unpublished studies. Studies meeting the eligibility criteria were retrieved and their methodological quality was assessed by 2 independent reviewers using the JBI critical appraisal checklists for randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies. Quantitative data were extracted using the standardized data extraction tool. Studies were pooled for statistical meta-analysis. Effect sizes were expressed as final post-intervention standardized mean differences, and their 95% CI were calculated. Heterogeneity was assessed statistically using the standard χ2 and I2 tests. Statistical analyses were performed using random-effects models and fixed-effect models. Where statistical pooling was not possible, the findings were presented in narrative format. A total of 34 studies met the inclusion criteria, with a total of 22,679 adolescents. Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials showed statistically significant differences for sleep knowledge (SMD=0.99, 95% CI=0.48 to 1.50, P<0.001), sleep hygiene (SMD=-0.20, 95% CI=-0.31 to -0.09, P=0.0003), and depressive symptoms (SMD=-0.70, 95% CI=-1.12 to -0.29, P<0.001). No statistically significant differences were found for sleep quality (SMD=0.06, 95% CI=-0.16 to 0.27, P=0.62), sleep efficiency (SMD=0.12, 95% CI=-0.02 to 0.26, P=0.09), sleep behavior-total sleep time/sleep duration (SMD=0.69, 95% CI=-0.27 to 1.65, P=0.16), and sleep behavior-sleep onset latency (SMD=-0.88, 95% CI=-1.77 to 0.01, P=0.05). Large effect sizes were observed for sleep knowledge and sleep onset latency; moderate-to-large effects for depressive symptoms and total sleep time; and small effects for sleep hygiene, sleep efficiency, and sleep quality. The funnel plot for sleep knowledge did not suggest publication bias, and Egger's test was not statistically significant. These findings suggest that school-based sleep promotion programs can be effective in improving adolescents' sleep knowledge and sleep hygiene, and reduce depressive symptoms. However, the high variability in intervention designs and methodological quality highlights the need for further high-quality studies to identify the most effective components of these programs and clarify their long-term impacts. PROSPERO CRD42023374838. A Portuguese-language translation of the abstract of this review is available: https://links.lww.com/SRX/A197.

papers.title: Photophysical and quenching principles governing advanced materials for fluorescence-based biosensing: mechanisms and analytical performance.
papers.abstract: Optical fluorescence biosensing has emerged as one of the most powerful strategies for ultrasensitive molecular detection, driven by rapid advances in fluorophore engineering, nanomaterial design, and signal-transduction architectures. At the core of these technologies lie fundamental excited-state processes, including fluorescence emission, Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET), photoinduced electron transfer (PET), and intramolecular charge transfer (ICT), that govern the generation, modulation, and detection of optical signals. In this review, we present a photophysics-centered framework for understanding and designing fluorescence-based biosensing processes, systematically correlating excited-state dynamics with analytical sensing performance. We examine a broad range of fluorescent materials, including organic dyes, semiconductor and metal quantum dots, perovskite nanocrystals, transition-metal complexes, lanthanide emitters, and emerging carbon-based nanodots, highlighting how their emission characteristics, quantum yields, photostability, and surface chemistry influence sensing capabilities. Particular emphasis is placed on fluorescence quenching mechanisms and the role of advanced quenching platforms including graphene derivatives, metal oxides, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), covalent organic frameworks (COFs), and hybrid nanostructures in tuning sensitivity, selectivity, and detection limits. Beyond material systems, we discuss recent progress in device integration and analytical methodologies, including microfluidic architectures, smartphone-enabled sensing platforms, nanophotonic metasurfaces, and artificial-intelligence-assisted spectral analysis, which are accelerating the translation of fluorescence biosensing toward portable and high-throughput applications. Despite these advances, challenges such as photobleaching, spectral interference, surface heterogeneity, and manufacturing reproducibility continue to affect analytical reliability. Emerging strategies based on defect-engineered two-dimensional materials, hybrid optical modalities, and machine-learning-driven signal interpretation are therefore highlighted as promising routes toward improved robustness and accuracy. By integrating photophysical principles, nanomaterial design, and analytical performance metrics into a unified perspective, this review provides a conceptual roadmap for the rational development of next-generation fluorescence-based biosensing technologies.

papers.title: PEDOT:PSS-Based OECT Common-Source Amplifiers for Electrophysiological Signal Amplification.
papers.abstract: Stable amplification of weak electrophysiological signals is important for low-voltage bioelectronic interfaces, but the gain and waveform fidelity of organic electrochemical transistor (OECT)-based amplifiers are strongly influenced by device characteristics and bias conditions. Herein, we develop a poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS) vertical organic electrochemical transistor (vOECT) common-source amplifier using an integrated solid-state electrolyte and investigate its bias-dependent amplification behavior. The fabricated vOECTs exhibits typical p-type depletion-mode operation, effective gate-controlled current modulation, and a maximum transconductance of 22 mS. Transient measurements show reversible current switching with response time constants of 0.909 and 0.635 ms, while repeated gate-voltage modulation over approximately 1000 s confirms stable cycling behavior. Based on the measured transfer and output characteristics, a common-source amplifier model is constructed to analyze the relationship between gate bias, bias resistance, output swing, and voltage gain. By optimizing the voltage-divider bias network, the amplifier achieves a voltage gain of approximately 3.374. The optimized circuit amplifies sinusoidal signals from 1 to 100 Hz and simulated ECG, EEG, and EOG waveforms while preserving their main temporal features and producing the expected phase-inverted output. Distortion and frequency-response analyses further show a 1% total harmonic distortion point at an input peak amplitude of 113 mV and a -3 dB cut-off frequency of 625 Hz. These results demonstrate the importance of bias optimization for achieving stable low-frequency voltage amplification in PEDOT:PSS vOECT common-source amplifiers.

papers.title: Genetic pleiotropy highlights immune mechanisms that link insomnia and C-reactive protein.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a prevalent sleep disorder with growing evidence implicating immune and inflammatory processes. Elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), a marker of systemic inflammation, is frequently observed in individuals with poor sleep, yet the genetic basis of this relationship remains unclear. This study aims to characterize the shared genetic architecture between insomnia and CRP using large-scale genomic data. CRP levels were significantly elevated in 130 611 individuals with insomnia compared with 327 375 controls in the UK Biobank. Genome-wide genetic correlation, pleiotropic analysis, colocalization, Mendelian randomization (MR), and functional annotation were used to characterize shared genetic architecture and biological pathways. Insomnia and CRP showed a significant positive genetic correlation. We identified 125 pleiotropic loci jointly associated with insomnia and CRP. Functional annotation implicated chromatin organization and nucleosome assembly, while pathway analyses highlighted immune signaling, cellular senescence, and programmed cell death. Colocalization analysis provided support for shared causal variants at six loci in or near APOE, HLA-B, NLGN1, AK5/DNAJB4, FAM114A2/GRIA1, and SATB1. Bidirectional MR provided stronger evidence for a directional relationship from insomnia liability to elevated CRP than in the reverse direction. This study uncovers shared genetic mechanisms linking insomnia and systemic inflammation. The directional genetic relationship from insomnia liability to elevated CRP suggests that sleep dysfunction may contribute to inflammatory processes.

papers.title: Symptoms of anxiety are linked to N3 sleep and lower dissipation of slow-wave activity during nocturnal sleep.
papers.abstract: Slow-wave sleep (SWS) is vital for brain health, memory, and emotional resilience. Slow-wave activity (SWA) reflects homeostatic sleep pressure, which dissipates across successive sleep cycles. Impaired SWA dissipation has been linked to depression. We examined whether reduced SWA dissipation is associated with symptoms of anxiety and depression in healthy conscripts. Seventy conscripts (67 males, aged 18-24) undergoing compulsory military service participated in overnight polysomnography. SWA dissipation was assessed by comparing normalized delta (0.5-4.0 Hz) electroencephalogram power between first and third NREM sleep episodes. This was complemented by full spectral analysis of sleep stages. Psychological measures included Overall Anxiety Severity and Impairment Scale, Beck's Depression Inventory, and Epworth Sleepiness Scale. Conscripts with elevated anxiety (24%) exhibited weaker SWA dissipation and greater proportion of N3 sleep. Similarly, anxiety was negatively correlated with SWA dissipation and positively with proportion of N3. Additionally, conscripts with elevated anxiety but without elevated depressiveness had less REM sleep than those with both anxiety and depression, as well as those without symptoms. Findings related to sleepiness or depression without anxiety were limited. In full spectral analysis individuals with higher anxiety exhibited elevated alpha power during REM sleep, potentially reflecting cortical hyperarousal. Higher proportion of N3 sleep and lower SWA dissipation were associated with greater anxiety rather than depression. These findings highlight the importance of adequate SWS in emotion regulation. Impaired SWA dissipation may contribute to preservation of negative emotional memories during sleep. Another possibility is that hyperarousal increases need for recovery sleep.

papers.title: Distinct Visual Pathways of Threat Retrieval in Fear-Conditioned Faces.
papers.abstract: Many have demonstrated rapid (< 100 ms) visuo-cortical differentiation of threat-associated faces. This may go back to low-spatial frequency (LSF) visual information originating from magnocellular pathways. Yet it remains unknown whether potentially magnocellular fear signals extend beyond evolutionarily prepared emotional faces. If so, spatial frequency characteristics should modulate visual processing of faces with newly acquired threat-relevance. Furthermore, it is unclear whether sub-bands of the visual spectrum are associated with autonomic arousal. Using a differential fear-conditioning paradigm (n = 68), this study tested whether early visual attentional capture, indicated by the P1 event-related potential component, face encoding, indicated by the N1 component, and autonomic arousal, indicated by skin conductance responses (SCR), prioritizes LSF information of threat-associated faces with neutral expressions during fear retrieval. Additionally, correlations tested whether the same subcortical system underlies the P1 and SCR. Stimulus ratings and N1 amplitudes confirmed successful fear acquisition. During fear retrieval, the P1 showed a selective left-hemispheric enhancement in response to LSF threat-faces. By contrast, the N1 was sensitive to spatial frequency but not fear-relevance. CS-differentiation in the SCR was not modulated by spatial frequency but longer CS presentations resulting in larger fear differentiation. Amplitudes of P1 and SCR were positively correlated only for safety faces. Data support the notion that magnocellular-cortical pathways adapt quickly to novel threat-associations and facilitate rapid threat retrieval in early visual attention, but not face encoding, even for perceptually neutral faces. At least in the present paradigm, subcortical fear pathways do not associate with anticipatory arousal in SCR.

papers.title: Menopausal symptom severities and patterns are affected by medical profiles.
papers.abstract: This study involved a secondary data analysis of Health & Her app data to investigate medical profiles and menopausal symptom clusters. Using a linear mixed effects model, we assessed how medical conditions, including Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS), premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), premature ovarian insufficiency (POI), cancers, depression, anxiety, uterine fibroids, endometriosis, adenomyosis and autoimmune disorders, predict menopausal symptom patterns. We also assessed medical procedures including bilateral oophorectomy, hysterectomy, unilateral oophorectomy, partial hysterectomy, endometrial ablation, and cancer treatment. Symptom clusters were identified via Principal Component Analysis. Linear mixed effects models analysed the effects of predictors on symptom outcomes. Menopausal symptom clusters, and how menopausal symptom patterns and severities are associated with medical profiles. Data from 210,489 app users from October 2020 to June 2024 identified symptom clusters, including joint aches, sleeping problems, low libido, weight gain, vasomotor, psychological/cognitive, vaginal and physical symptoms. Depression and anxiety were associated with the strongest increases in menopausal symptoms. Gynaecological surgeries were associated with increased vasomotor symptoms. POI and endometriosis were associated with vaginal symptoms. Autoimmune diseases had significant associations with joint aches, and physical and psychological/cognitive symptoms. PMOS, adenomyosis and PMDD were associated with reduced vasomotor symptoms. Undergoing cancer treatment was associated with reduced symptoms in most domains, albeit vaginal and vasomotor symptoms increased. Likewise, breast and gynaecological cancers were associated with low libido, and increased vasomotor and sleep symptoms. Our findings highlight the importance of healthcare professionals considering comorbidities when supporting women with menopausal symptoms.

papers.title: Circadian timing does not modulate human temporal contrast sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Previous studies have reported diurnal variations in color perception and luminance contrast sensitivity, suggesting modulation of visual processing by the circadian pacemaker. To clarify potential time-of-day effects, we examined whether cone-mediated temporal contrast sensitivity is modulated by circadian timing. We disentangled circadian and homeostatic influences on human visual performance using a 40-hour forced desynchrony protocol. Twelve participants (five female participants, 24.4 ± 2.9 years, range 19-30) followed a repeating 3.75-hour cycle comprising 2 hours 30 minutes of wakefulness and 1 hour 15 minutes of sleep under constant environmental conditions. Circadian period was estimated from up to 46 salivary melatonin samples per participant. During wake periods, participants repeatedly completed temporal contrast sensitivity tasks at 2 Hz and 8 Hz, using tasks that probed both luminance (L+M+S) and chromatic (L-M, S-cone-directed) modulations. We tested for circadian modulation of visual performance by comparing hierarchical cosinor models with intercept-only null models using Bayes factors. All participants showed robust melatonin rhythms (mean τ = 24.18 ± 0.39 hours). Bayesian inference provided decisive evidence against circadian variation in luminance or chromatic contrast sensitivity. Within this controlled protocol, we found no detectable near-24-hour modulation of cone-mediated temporal contrast sensitivity. Previously reported time-of-day effects may instead reflect homeostatic influences, pupil-linked changes in retinal illuminance, or mechanisms outside the cone-mediated pathways probed here. By separating circadian phase from sleep-wake-related influences, this study clarifies when circadian modulation of visual performance can and cannot be inferred.

papers.title: Mild acute sleep restriction alters visual attention during driving: an eye-tracking study using a driving simulator.
papers.abstract: Safe driving requires cognitive resources such as attention, working memory, and decision-making. Sleep loss impacts these resources, affecting driving performance. Although severe or chronic sleep deprivation is well-studied, the impact of the far more common, mild and acute sleep loss remains less well understood. Similarly, current eye tracking technology in passenger vehicles relies on eye closures or head position as a marker of drowsiness. But these are downstream indicators of fitness to drive. Eye fixation patterns may be a more sensitive, early warning sign of drowsiness. Eye movements were studied to identify patterns (i.e., fixations) reflecting reduced cognitive and behavioral performance during a driving simulation, related to mild sleep loss from the previous night. It was hypothesized that even a single night of reduced sleep would reduce vigilance and impair driving performance, with oculomotor features serving as physiological markers of these deficits. Twenty-two participants completed 1-h driving simulations requiring sustained attention and quick responses under two conditions: while normally rested, or after mild sleep restriction. Sleep restriction led to slower response times, increased lapses and crashes, and altered eye fixation patterns across different driving demands (e.g., tailgating or not) that reflect cognitive processing of the environment. These findings suggest that eye fixations may be useful indicators of driver fatigue and reduced driving fitness related to mild acute sleep loss. These results provide insight into the underlying cognitive processes that may be associated with sleep loss-related fitness to drive.

papers.title: Multimodal Evidence for Large-scale Network Imbalance in Etomidate Use Disorder.
papers.abstract: Etomidate use disorder (EUD) is an escalating public health issue in East and Southeast Asia, yet its neuroimaging features remain poorly understood. This study used simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to examine multimodal functional connectivity alterations in individuals with EUD. A total of 54 individuals with EUD and 46 healthy controls (HCs) were recruited and underwent simultaneous resting-state EEG and fNIRS recordings. Psychological dimensions including impulsivity, aggression, and craving were evaluated using standardized and validated scales. Source-level EEG functional connectivity and fNIRS hemodynamic connectivity were analyzed to identify group differences. Associations between altered connectivity features and clinical measures were examined within the EUD group. Machine learning analyses were conducted as exploratory assessments of the discriminative information contained in multimodal connectivity features. In unadjusted exploratory analyses of BIS-11 and BPAQ subscales, the EUD group showed higher cognitive impulsivity, non-planning impulsivity, physical aggression, anger and self-directed aggression (t=2.32 to 4.54, p<0.05), but lower motor impulsivity, compared with HCs. Source-level EEG analysis revealed significant group differences only in the delta band, with reduced large-scale connectivity in EUD involving default mode, dorsal attention, visual and sensorimotor systems. fNIRS analysis showed reduced hemodynamic connectivity across multiple frontal subregions and motor-related areas. Weaker connectivity between the primary motor cortex and the triangular part of the inferior frontal gyrus was associated with stronger negative reinforcement craving (rho=-0.471, p_FDR<0.05). Exploratory machine learning analysis showed preliminary discriminative performance, with the random forest model producing the numerically highest test-set AUC (0.80) in this particular data split. Convergent EEG-fNIRS findings suggest delta-band network decoupling and reduced frontal hemodynamic connectivity as multimodal neural features of EUD. These findings provide preliminary evidence for the neural mechanisms of EUD and may inform future objective assessment and treatment-monitoring studies.

papers.title: Short-Term Prognosis in Adolescents and Adults with Major Depressive Disorder and Associated Psychosocial Factors: A Prospective Study.
papers.abstract: This prospective study examined whether short-term treatment outcomes differ between adolescents and adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) and evaluated the contribution of psychosocial factors to these differences. Adolescents and adults receiving treatment in the Department of Psychiatry were consecutively recruited between June 2023 and December 2024, including 115 adolescents (64.61%) and 63 adults (35.39%) in the final week-8 analysis set. Depressive symptom severity was assessed using the 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-24). Anhedonia, sleep quality, interpersonal functioning, and social support were evaluated using the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS), the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), the Interpersonal Relationship Scale (IRS), and the Social Support Rating Scale (SSRS), respectively. Assessments were completed at baseline and at 2, 4, and 8 weeks after treatment initiation. At baseline, the two groups differed in educational attainment and illness duration (P < 0.05), whereas HAMD-24 scores were comparable. Sleep-related measures showed limited between-group differences, but adolescents reported more severe anhedonia, poorer interpersonal functioning, and lower social support than adults (P < 0.05). After 8 weeks of treatment, HAMD-24 scores decreased significantly in both groups, but adults achieved higher remission and overall effectiveness rates than adolescents (P < 0.001). In both age groups, poorer interpersonal functioning and lower social support were associated with less favorable prognosis, with stronger associations observed in adolescents. These findings suggest that psychosocial disadvantage may weigh more heavily on short-term treatment outcomes in adolescent MDD. Interventions that strengthen interpersonal functioning and social support may therefore be particularly relevant for improving prognosis in this population.

papers.title: Effects of 30- and 90-Minute Afternoon Nap Opportunities on Field-Test Performance in Female Collegiate Basketball Players.
papers.abstract: Afternoon napping is used as a recovery strategy in sport, but a scheduled nap opportunity is not equivalent to objectively verified sleep. This study compared no-nap seated wakefulness (N0), a 30-minute scheduled nap opportunity (N30), and a 90-minute scheduled nap opportunity (N90) in 18 female collegiate basketball players using a randomized, fully counterbalanced, three-period within-participant crossover design. Conditions were separated by at least 72 h and ended at 14:30, followed by a common 60 min wakefulness buffer, a standardized 15 min warm-up, and a fixed basketball field-test battery. Linear mixed-effects models included condition, period, and sequence as fixed effects, with participant as a random intercept; the nine omnibus condition tests were controlled for using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. Four of nine outcomes remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction: the modified-505 first 10 m split, combined modified-505 completion time, three-quarter-court sprint time, and 30-15 Intermittent Fitness Test final velocity. N90 differed from both N0 and N30 for these outcomes, whereas N30 did not differ from N0. The other five outcomes did not meet the false-discovery-rate threshold. Sensitivity analyses, including reanalysis of the pre-correction modified-505 data, preserved the same four-outcome pattern. Because sleep onset and duration were not objectively measured, the findings estimate the effects of assigned recovery-opportunity conditions rather than a physiological sleep-duration dose-response.

papers.title: Financial Toxicity and Follow-Up Quality of Life Among Breast Cancer Survivors in the BOLD Cohort.
papers.abstract: Financial toxicity is prevalent in cancer survivorship and has been associated with poorer health-related quality of life (HRQOL), yet longitudinal evidence remains limited. We examined associations between financial toxicity and HRQOL at baseline and 4-month follow-up among breast cancer survivors in the BOLD cohort. Data were drawn from self-report questionnaires completed by 182 breast cancer survivors at baseline, of whom 146 completed 4-month follow-up surveys. Financial toxicity was assessed at baseline using the Comprehensive Score for Financial Toxicity (COST). HRQOL outcomes were assessed at baseline and approximately 4 months later using the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy-General (FACT-G) subscales and total score, and a single-item measure of sleep disturbance. Multivariable linear regression models estimated adjusted cross-sectional associations and longitudinal associations between baseline financial toxicity and follow-up outcomes, adjusting for baseline levels of the corresponding outcome. Longitudinal measurement invariance of the COST was evaluated. Greater baseline financial toxicity was associated with lower baseline physical, social/family, emotional, and functional well-being, lower FACT-G total score, and greater sleep disturbance. In longitudinal models, higher baseline financial toxicity was associated with lower follow-up physical, social/family, emotional, and functional well-being and lower FACT-G total score after adjustment for demographic and clinical covariates and the corresponding baseline outcome. Baseline financial toxicity was not associated with follow-up sleep disturbance. Financial toxicity was associated with poorer HRQOL at baseline and with lower physical, social/family, emotional, functional, and overall HRQOL at follow-up. These findings support greater attention to financial toxicity in survivorship care.

papers.title: Associations Between Resting-State EEG Delta-band Activity at Selected Parietal Electrodes and Cognitive Changes Following Transcutaneous Auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation in Patients with Mild Cognitive Impairment: An Exploratory Analysis.
papers.abstract: Transcutaneous auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation (taVNS) may improve cognition in Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), but its electrophysiological correlates remain unclear. We explored whether parietal delta-band changes were associated with cognitive changes following taVNS. This exploratory secondary analysis included 26 participants with MCI from a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial (taVNS, n = 14; sham, n = 12) who had valid resting-state EEG data at baseline and Week 24. Absolute and relative 1-3 Hz delta power at Pz, P1, P2, and P5 were analyzed using repeated-measures ANOVA and EEG-cognitive correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction. Absolute delta power showed significant time effects at all four electrodes after FDR correction (all q = 0.008). Relative delta power at Pz showed an uncorrected group effect (F = 5.007, p = 0.035; q = 0.218). In the taVNS group, MoCA-B improvement was positively associated with relative delta-power changes at P1, P2, and P5 (r = 0.629-0.652, p = 0.012-0.016), whereas AVLTN7 improvement was negatively associated with absolute delta-power changes across Pz, P1, P2, and P5 (coefficients = -0.418 to -0.613, p = 0.020-0.048). Although these correlations did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple comparisons, they showed a relatively consistent direction across multiple electrodes. Relative and absolute delta power may reflect complementary aspects of spectral modulation. The convergent cross-electrode associations provide preliminary EEG evidence linked to cognitive response to taVNS. Parietal delta-band power may represent a candidate electrophysiological marker of cognitive change following taVNS in MCI. These exploratory findings support further validation of predefined EEG biomarkers in larger, prospectively powered studies. http://www.chictr.org.cn (ID: ChiCTR2000038868).

papers.title: Chronotherapeutic and Circadian Rhythm-Based Strategies in Diabetes Management: A Critical Opinion Based on Evidences.
papers.abstract: Diabetes mellitus is one of the world's leading health problems, and standard approaches to therapy do not take into consideration the impact of circadian misalignment on metabolic health. Chronobiological processes are involved in regulating glucose homeostasis, insulin release, hepatic glucose production, lipids, and energy metabolism; hence, disruptions such as those caused by non-rhythmic sleep patterns, shifts at work, irregular meal times, and light exposure could cause insulin resistance and even type 2 diabetes. The current critical review discusses the light-melatonin interaction and personalized chronobiological medicine. Instead of giving a descriptive account of particular treatments, the paper introduces the integrative importance of chronobiology for the management of diabetes by considering data about chrononutrition, time-restricted feeding, chronopharmacology, chrono-exercise, and an approach to chronometabolism based on the integration of the timing of meals, drugs, exercise, sleep, and light exposure with chronotype, metabolic phenotype, and the feasibility of the therapy. Circadian timing can be a promising adjuvant in the treatment of diabetes; however, the available evidence does not suggest an ideal time for intervention. Further studies should focus on measuring time, well-powered randomized controlled trials, long-term outcomes, and individualization of chronotherapy.

papers.title: Robust Functional Ward's Linkages With Applications in EEG Data Clustering.
papers.abstract: This paper proposes two robust linkage criteria, termed functional Ward-type linkages, for hierarchical clustering of grouped functional data, where each clustering unit is represented by a set of curves. Ordinary Ward's linkage defines the cluster dissimilarity between two clusters as the increase in the sum of squared errors (SSE) upon merging, which can be interpreted graphically as an increase in within-cluster dispersion. Motivated by this principle, the proposed linkages measure the weighted increase in band width required to construct a common band containing the central representatives of two candidate clusters. To reduce the influence of outliers, the central curves are selected separately within each cluster by leveraging the magnitude-shape outlyingness measure and the modified band depth, respectively. Simulations and two EEG data analyses demonstrate the robustness and competitive performance of the proposed methods under a range of contamination settings.

papers.title: Effects of temperature on the growth, development, and reproduction of Cyamophila willieti (Hemiptera: Psyllidae) evaluated using the age-stage, two-sex life table.
papers.abstract: The study examined key biological and ecological traits of Cyamophila willieti, a major pest of Styphnolobium japonicum, including its circadian mating rhythm, oviposition preference, and temperature-dependent population performance. Using the age-stage, two-sex life table approach, we compared the development, reproduction, and population growth potential of C. willieti under three temperature regimes. Results showed that mating activity followed a bimodal circadian rhythm with peaks at 12:00 and 17:00, while females showed a strong preference for ovipositing on shoot tips. C. willieti achieved higher population growth rates at 25 °C compared to 29 °C and 33 °C, with an intrinsic rate of increase (r) of 0.1885 ± 0.0086 day-1, a finite rate of increase (λ) of 1.2075 ± 0.0104 day-1, a net reproductive rate (R0) of 215.92 ± 43.00 offspring per individual, a mean longevity of 35.03 ± 2.02 days, and a fecundity of 647.75 ± 52.94 eggs per female. Compared with 29 °C, r, R0, and fecundity were 2.95-, 34.0-, and 13.6-fold higher at 25 °C, respectively, whereas most nymphs failed to develop beyond the fifth instar at 33 °C. Our results suggest that 25 °C was more favourable for the development, reproduction, and population growth of C. willieti than the higher temperatures of 29 °C and 33 °C, providing a basis for its monitoring and sustainable management.

papers.title: Association Between the Time of Day of Post-Transplant Cyclophosphamide Administration and Haemorrhagic Cystitis After Allogeneic Haematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the impact of the time-of-day (daytime vs. nighttime) of the infusion of post-transplantation cyclophosphamide (PTCy) on the occurrence of haemorrhagic cystitis (HC) in adult patients undergoing allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT). We conducted a retrospective, single-centre cohort study including adult allo-HSCT between January 2014 and December 2022. All patients received PTCy at a dose of 50 mg/kg/day for two consecutive days. Patients were classified according to the timing of the first PTCy dose: daytime (06:00-17:59) or nighttime (18:00-05:59). The primary endpoint was the incidence of Grade II-IV HC. A total of 178 patients were included. Grade II-IV HC occurred in 16.4% and 31.2% of patients following daytime and nighttime administration, respectively (OR 2.31, 95% CI 0.97-5.49; p = 0.079). After adjustment for potential confounders, nighttime administration was associated with higher odds of Grade II-IV HC (adjusted OR 2.82, 95% CI 1.12-7.10; p = 0.028). Grade III-IV HC was more frequent following nighttime administration (4.8% vs. 15.6%; OR 3.68, 95% CI 1.09-12.45; p = 0.043). No significant differences were observed in transplant outcomes. Nighttime administration of PTCy was associated with a numerically higher incidence of Grade II-IV HC, although the unadjusted primary analysis did not reach conventional statistical significance. This association was statistically significant after adjustment for potential confounders. No detectable differences in transplant outcomes were observed. These findings support prospective evaluation of chronomodulated PTCy administration as a simple, potentially modifiable strategy for reducing treatment-related toxicity after allo-HSCT.

papers.title: Drug treatments for fibromyalgia: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials.
papers.abstract: To compare the effectiveness of drug treatments for the management of fibromyalgia. Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials. Medline, Embase, AMED (Allied and Complementary Medicine Database), PsycInfo, CINAHL, and Cochrane CENTRAL (Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials), from inception to 13 January 2025. Parallel, crossover, and cluster randomised trials that enrolled adults (aged ≥18 years) with fibromyalgia, according to any published diagnostic criteria or as diagnosed by a physician. Trials compared commercially available, investigational, or discontinued drug treatments with another drug, the same drug at a different dose or regimen, placebo, or standard care. Treatments also included select vitamins and supplements, such as melatonin, vitamin D, vitamin B6, and omega 3 fatty acids. 151 eligible trials (32 592 participants) were included in this systematic review. Compared with placebo or usual care, low certainty evidence suggested that sodium oxybate, selective noradrenaline (norepinephrine) reuptake inhibitors (NRIs), serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs), and gabapentinoids may increase the likelihood of patient reported meaningful improvement or recovery (risk difference 105 to 283 more per 1000 patients). Based on scores from the fibromyalgia impact questionnaire, low certainty evidence further suggested that sodium oxybate (mean difference -8.81, 95% confidence interval (CI) -11.78 to -5.84) and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) (mean difference -8.02, 95% CI -13.40 to -2.64) may reduce fibromyalgia symptoms, whereas tricyclic antidepressants, sodium oxybate, and gabapentinoids may improve sleep quality. No drug showed pooled effects on pain, physical health or mental health that met or exceeded a threshold for clinical importance. For sodium oxybate, selective NRIs, SNRIs, and cyclobenzaprine, responder analyses indicated that a potentially important proportion of patients achieved a reduction in pain of at least 30% (risk difference 111 to 202 more per 1000 patients). In addition, no drug increased the risk of discontinuing treatment or serious adverse events. This systematic review and network meta-analysis provides low certainty evidence that sodium oxybate, selective NRIs, SNRIs, gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants, and SSRIs may provide typically small benefits in select outcomes for people with fibromyalgia. PROSPERO CRD42012003291.

papers.title: A Study on Work-Related Injuries and Its Association with Sleep Quality and Other Related Factors Among Firefighters in the District of Kollam, Kerala.
papers.abstract: Firefighters perform high-risk, physically demanding duties with irregular hours and disrupted sleep, increasing injury risk. This study assessed the burden of work-related injuries and their association with sleep quality among firefighters in Kollam, Kerala. An institution-based cross-sectional study was conducted from September 2024 to November 2025 among 106 firefighters from all 11 Fire and Rescue stations, selected by simple random sampling. Data were collected through face-to-face interviews using a pre-tested structured questionnaire and analyzed using Microsoft Excel 2021 and JAMOVI 2.5.4. Among 106 male firefighters (median age 39; IQR 37-43), 76.4% were married, 62.3% graduates, and 70.8% upper socioeconomic class. Alcohol use (29.2%), and smoking (17%) were reported; all used personal protective equipment (PPE) and 66% had normal body mass index (BMI). Participants worked ≥72 hours weekly with daily physical training. Weekly hazardous exposure was reported by 41.5% and related health problems by 53.8%. Work-related injuries occurred in 39.6%, mostly mild (61.9%) and limb-related (50%), commonly during fire and rescue operations, with fatigue as the leading contributor (40.5%). Poor sleep quality (55.7%) showed a significant association with injury (P < 0.001). Work-related injuries are common among firefighters and are strongly associated with poor sleep quality. Optimizing duty schedules, strengthening workplace safety, and promoting sleep health may help reduce injuries.

papers.title: Intermittent theta-burst stimulation versus sham stimulation for suicidal ideation and psychiatric symptoms in depressive disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: Suicidal ideation, depressive symptoms, anxiety, and sleep disturbance remain difficult to manage in psychiatric populations, and intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) has emerged as an accelerated, non-invasive neuromodulation strategy for these outcomes. This meta-analysis compares iTBS versus sham-iTBS across suicidal ideation, depression severity, anxiety severity, and sleep quality to guide clinical decision-making. We systematically searched relevant electronic databases in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Continuous outcomes were pooled as standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals using random-effects inverse-variance models in RevMan 5.4. Heterogeneity was assessed using I 2 and χ 2 statistics, and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were performed. A p value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Six studies were included. iTBS significantly reduced suicidal ideation versus sham-iTBS (SMD = -0.51; 95% CI: -0.93 to -0.09; p = 0.02; I 2 = 70%; n = 181 vs. 157), and the effect remained significant with lower heterogeneity after exclusion of Qin et al. (p = 0.02; I 2 = 29%). Depression severity improved with iTBS (SMD = -1.06; 95% CI: -1.64 to -0.48; p = 0.0003; I 2 = 80%; n = 162 vs. 142), with heterogeneity decreasing to 24% after exclusion of Huang et al. Anxiety severity also improved (SMD = -0.68; 95% CI: -1.27 to -0.09; p = 0.02; I 2 = 79%; n = 139 vs. 120), and heterogeneity decreased to 38% after exclusion of Huang et al. Sleep quality did not differ significantly between groups (SMD = -0.32; 95% CI: -0.98 to 0.34; p = 0.35; I 2 = 67%; n = 75 vs. 49), based on two trials. iTBS was associated with a reduction in suicidal ideation compared with sham stimulation, but the small evidence base and between-study heterogeneity limit certainty. Secondary analyses suggested improvements in depression and anxiety severity, whereas sleep quality did not differ between groups. Larger, standardized randomized controlled trials with longer follow-up are needed to determine the magnitude and durability of any antisuicidal effect.
