papers.title: Joint-brain communication in rheumatoid arthritis: glial mechanisms, pain phenotypes, and translational evidence.
papers.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic autoimmune disease in which persistent pain, fatigue, cognitive impairment, depression, and anxiety may involve altered central nervous system (CNS) processing. This narrative review synthesizes preclinical and clinical evidence concerning proposed glial cell-mediated joint-brain communication in RA. Joint-derived neural inputs and systemic inflammatory signals may communicate with the CNS through humoral, cellular, neural, neuroendocrine, and neurovascular pathways. Preclinical studies implicate microglia and astrocytes in neuroinflammatory responses, spinal central sensitization, impaired hippocampal plasticity, and neurovascular alterations. Human studies associate systemic inflammation with altered brain connectivity and CNS-related symptoms. Disease-modifying antirheumatic treatment, particularly tumor necrosis factor inhibition, has been associated with improvements in selected CNS-related outcomes. Adjunctive symptom management includes phenotype-guided analgesic approaches, rehabilitation, and psychological and sleep-focused interventions. Translational research explores glial modulators, pathway-specific interventions, vagal neuromodulation, neuroimaging, cerebrospinal fluid markers, and multidimensional patient stratification. The proposed joint-brain framework highlights the value of assessing inflammation alongside pain phenotype, cognition, mood, fatigue, sleep, and function. Future human studies should evaluate whether mechanistic and biomarker findings can improve individualized treatment selection and clinical outcomes.

papers.title: Sleep-inflammation-coronary plaque phenotype axis: clinical validation and inflammation-mediated mechanisms based on optical coherence tomography.
papers.abstract: The influence of sleep duration on vulnerable coronary plaques, as evaluated via optical coherence tomography (OCT), has not been clearly defined in coronary artery disease (CAD). Here, the relationships between habitual sleep duration and thin-cap fibroatheroma (TCFA) detected by OCT were investigated in individuals with CAD. We further investigated whether systemic inflammation, represented by the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), represents a mediator of this association. Overall, 1,178 patients with angiographically confirmed CAD who underwent OCT imaging and completed standardized sleep questionnaires were enrolled. Participants were categorized according to reported sleep duration. Multivariable logistic regression modeling was employed to assess the link between sleep duration and TCFA. Linear regression analyses assessed the association between sleep duration and NLR. Restricted cubic spline (RCS) modeling was applied as a means of detecting possible nonlinear associations between NLR and TCFA. Mediation analyses were then conducted to determine whether NLR functioned as an intermediate variable linking sleep duration and plaque vulnerability. These results offer the first clinical evidence of the link between sleep duration and TCFA presence in individuals with CAD, with the TCFA risk in the abnormal sleep duration group being 2.16 times that of the normal group (95% CI: 1.63-2.88, P < 0.001). Sleep duration was also independently correlated with NLR, and RCS analysis highlighted a nonlinear relationship between NLR levels and TCFA risk (P < 0.001). Importantly, mediation analysis demonstrated that NLR partially mediated the effect of sleep duration on TCFA, supporting the existence of a sleep-inflammation-plaque vulnerability axis. The sleep duration has been shown to be significantly associated with the risk of developing TCFA. In addition, a partial mediating effect of NLR on this relationship has been found.

papers.title: Developing and Validating a Parent Guide to Improve Sleep in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder: Emphasis on the Holistic Approach to Self-Regulation Strategies.
papers.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) frequently coexists with sleep problems. This study, guided by family-centered and general systems theories and acknowledging the reciprocal relationships between sleep and self-regulation, details the process of designing a parent guide aimed at improving sleep in children aged 6-12 years diagnosed with level 1 or 2 ASD. A literature search was conducted to identify interventions that emphasize self-regulation strategies aimed at improving children's sleep. The content and face validity of this guide were evaluated based on the opinions of experts and parents. In a pilot study, the guide was presented to parents of children with ASD (n = 3) in the form of a booklet, and its effectiveness was assessed through caregiver feedback and the Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ). The booklet comprises 23 subtitles organized into four chapters: "Introductory Information," "Child-Related Factors," "Environment-Related Factors," and "Impact of Other Activities on Sleep." In this feasibility pilot (n=3), minor reductions (2-3 points) in CSHQ scores were observed; however, this magnitude of change is below typical minimal clinically important differences, and the study was not designed to assess efficacy. The development of a parent guide for sleep of children with ASD was driven by the need to address self-regulatory strategies across three interrelated dimensions: the child, the environment, and sleep itself. This approach is superior to single-domain interventions that do not adequately consider the complex interplay of self-regulation deficits in ASD. This study provides initial evidence for the viability and promise of this intervention, paving the way for definitive future trials.

papers.title: Comprehensive Multimodal Diagnostics and Rehabilitation in Persistent Post-Concussion Syndrome Following Motor Vehicle Collision.
papers.abstract: Motor vehicle collisions (MVCs) are among the most common mechanisms of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), and a meaningful proportion of affected individuals develop persistent post-concussion syndrome (PPCS) characterized by prolonged multidomain dysfunction. Conventional neuroimaging frequently fails to capture the underlying pathophysiology, leaving clinicians without objective diagnostic evidence. We describe a 57-year-old woman who sustained mTBI in a rear-end MVC in March 2023. Head computed tomography (CT) performed at the emergency department and a subsequent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) were both unremarkable. Despite normal structural neuroimaging, comprehensive multimodal functional assessment identified functional abnormalities across eight domains: vestibular function (videonystagmography (VNG)), cortical electrophysiology (quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG)), pupillary autonomics (automated infrared pupillometry), postural stability (computerized dynamic posturography (CDP)), oculomotor control (saccadometry), cardiac autonomic regulation (24-h heart rate variability (HRV)), olfaction (University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test (UPSIT)), and computerized concussion assessment (C3 Logix). Standardized psychological assessments confirmed moderate depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) = 14), moderate anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) = 12), clinically significant post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms (PTSD Checklist for Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5) (PCL-5 = 38)), and substantial headache impact (Headache Impact Test-6 (HIT-6) = 58). The patient underwent a 10-modality individualized rehabilitation program. Concussion Symptom Checklist (CSC) scores declined from 92 at initial presentation to 0 by July 2023 (17 weeks post-injury), with near-complete re-resolution to 8 by February 2024 following a transient stress-related exacerbation. When conventional neuroimaging is unremarkable, comprehensive multimodal functional testing may provide evidence consistent with mTBI pathophysiology and help guide targeted rehabilitation. This case illustrates the potential value of a systematic, multimodal approach in PPCS management, while acknowledging that definitive attribution of findings to the index injury is constrained by the single-case design and absence of a pre-injury functional baseline.

papers.title: Neuropathic Pain: From Mechanisms to Therapeutic Interventions.
papers.abstract: Neuropathic pain is caused by injury or disease of the somatosensory system. It involves peripheral nerve injury, central sensitization, transmitter imbalance, glial activation, and large-scale network remodeling. Despite substantial advances in pain biology, clinical assessment continues to rely predominantly on patient-reported symptoms, sensory examination, and conventional neurophysiological testing, approaches that often fail to delineate the predominant biological mechanisms underlying pain in individual patients. Recent advances in sensory phenotyping and multimodal imaging have enabled in vivo characterization of abnormalities at the receptor, neuroinflammatory, and circuit levels, thereby providing a foundation for mechanism-based stratification and more individualized therapeutic decision-making. This review summarizes neuropathic pain from clinical stratification to mechanism-based imaging and therapeutic intervention. We describe key clinical dimensions, including sensory gain, sensory loss, peripheral and central pain generators, mixed nociceptive-neuropathic pain, central sensitization, and autonomic or small-fiber modifiers. These dimensions help explain why patients with the same diagnosis may show different symptoms and treatment responses. We also review major molecular mechanisms, including glutamatergic overactivity, GABAergic and glycinergic disinhibition, monoaminergic remodeling, and neuroimmune modulation. These changes reshape spinal, thalamocortical, limbic, salience, reward, cerebellar, and descending control circuits. Peripheral nerve ultrasound and MR neurography can help identify structural peripheral pain generators. PET, MRS, MRI, DTI, fMRI, EEG, and multimodal imaging can assess receptor availability, neurotransmitter balance, neuroinflammation, white matter integrity, and network connectivity. These imaging tools may link clinical phenotypes with biological mechanisms and help define mechanism-based subtypes. Imaging biomarkers may also support treatment selection, treatment monitoring, neuromodulation targeting, and translational trial design. This framework supports a shift from symptom-based assessment to mechanism-guided precision care for neuropathic pain.

papers.title: Exercise, Stress, Sleep, Job Satisfaction, and Burnout Among Indian Doctors: A Nationwide Occupational Health Study of 4,400 Physicians.
papers.abstract: Physician burnout is an occupational hazard driven by workload, fatigue, and poor recovery. Exercise and sleep enhance resilience, yet Indian data integrating behavioral and workplace factors are scarce. To examine how exercise, workload, stress, sleep quality, and job satisfaction interact to predict burnout among Indian doctors. Nationwide cross-sectional, web-based survey conducted from January to June 2025. Four thousand and four hundred doctors (880 each from orthopedics, general surgery, anesthesiology, psychiatry, and internal medicine) were surveyed with equal gender and public-private distribution. A validated 24-item questionnaire (Cronbach's α = 0.86) assessed exercise, stress, sleep quality, job satisfaction, and burnout. SPSS 27.0; Chi-square, ANOVA, Pearson r, and multivariate regression (VIF <2). Regular exercise was reported by 78.2%. Orthopedic surgeons were most active (90%), psychiatrists least (68%). Burnout correlated positively with stress (r = 0.61) and workload (r = 0.29), and negatively with exercise (r = -0.36), sleep (r = -0.43), and satisfaction (r = -0.48). Moderate exercise (30-60 min/day) provided optimal sleep improvement and burnout reduction, with diminishing gains beyond 60 min. Job satisfaction buffered 38% of the exercise's effect on burnout. Exercise, sleep, and satisfaction independently protect against burnout, while excessive work and stress increase vulnerability. Balanced lifestyle and institutional wellness policies may improve occupational health and sustainability.

papers.title: Evaluation of Pompe Disease from a Broad and Systemic Perspective.
papers.abstract: Pompe disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by α-1,4-glucosidase deficiency. The broad spectrum of clinical manifestations results from glycogen accumulation in the muscles and central nervous system (CNS). In this study, we aimed to evaluate the clinical course of Pompe disease. This brief report included six patients. The collected data included demographic characteristics, clinical findings, echocardiography, electroencephalography, electromyography, and brain magnetic resonance imaging. High-dose enzyme replacement therapy reduced the severity of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in patients with infantile-onset Pompe disease. Three patients exhibited speech difficulties, one patient was diagnosed with epilepsy, and MRI revealed white matter abnormalities in three patients. The neurological findings observed in patients with CNS involvement suggest that those with infantile-onset Pompe disease should be closely monitored for neurocognitive development. Novel treatments capable of crossing the blood-brain barrier may benefit these patients.

papers.title: Thoracolumbar pain associated with cervical radiculopathy successfully managed with combined cervical periradicular injection and ultrasound-guided percutaneous electrical nerve stimulation therapy: a case report.
papers.abstract: Cervical radiculopathy may occasionally present with atypical pain patterns extending beyond the classical cervical and upper-limb distribution, potentially leading to diagnostic uncertainty. The thoracodorsal nerve originates predominantly from the C6-C8 roots and innervates the latissimus dorsi muscle, providing a possible anatomical basis for referred pain involving the posterior thoracolumbar region. This case describes an unusual presentation of cervical radiculopathy manifesting predominantly as severe thoracolumbar pain and its management using a combined interventional approach. A 74-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of severe right thoracolumbar pain, localized hyperalgesia, and painful myofascial tenderness involving the latissimus dorsi region. Baseline pain intensity was 8/10 on the numerical rating scale (NRS), with associated limitation of trunk mobility and sleep interruption. Previous pharmacological and rehabilitative treatments had failed to provide clinically significant improvement. Cervical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multilevel degenerative disc disease with right-sided foraminal stenosis involving the C6-C7 and C7-T1 levels. Ultrasound-guided periradicular steroid injections at the right C6, C7, and C8 levels produced significant pain reduction within 48 hours. Subsequently, two sessions of ultrasound-guided percutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (PENS) targeting the presumed thoracodorsal nerve pathway were performed over a 2-month period. At follow-up, pain intensity decreased to NRS 2/10, with improvement in trunk mobility and daily activities. No complications or adverse events were observed. This case highlights the importance of considering a possible cervical origin in selected patients presenting with otherwise unexplained thoracolumbar pain. The favorable clinical course observed after cervical periradicular injections followed by ultrasound-guided PENS suggests that this combined approach may represent a minimally invasive therapeutic strategy in selected patients with refractory cervicogenic thoracolumbar pain. Further studies are required to clarify the underlying mechanisms and determine the specific contribution of PENS to the observed clinical improvement.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Based Fatigue Detection from EEG Signals: A Methodological Pilot Framework with Potential for Nursing Applications.
papers.abstract: Fatigue is a significant occupational health issue that adversely affects attention and decision-making. This study aimed to objectively predict fatigue levels using EEG signals and machine learning models and to develop a physiologically based assessment framework with potential future applications in nursing. Time-domain, frequency-domain, entropy, Hjorth, and wavelet features were extracted from EEG data collected from 12 participants aged 21-40 years, with fatigue levels labeled using various scales. Classification performance varied across validation strategies. Under 5-fold cross-validation, Random Forest achieved the highest performance (accuracy=1.00, macro-F1=1.00), while KNN and NB also demonstrated strong performance. However, under LOOCV, sensitivity, precision, and macro-F1 values decreased despite relatively high accuracy. LOSO validation yielded more balanced results, with Random Forest maintaining the best performance (accuracy=0.97, macro-F1=0.91). EEG-derived features provide valuable information for fatigue assessment. Although high performance was achieved under certain validation strategies, subject-independent evaluation revealed more realistic performance levels. The proposed framework offers a practical approach to fatigue monitoring. Future studies should focus on larger, domain-specific datasets and multimodal integration to enhance generalizability.
papers.journal: Journal of clinical practice and research

papers.title: Cognitive-emotional associations between non-restorative sleep and erectile dysfunction: the role of rumination profiles and resilience.
papers.abstract: Erectile dysfunction (ED) is a prevalent male health condition that substantially correlates with impaired sexual function and reduced overall quality of life. Non-restorative sleep (NRS), a prevalent subjective sleep disturbance, has recently been identified as an under-recognized factor linked to ED. Nonetheless, the psychological factors involved in the association between NRS and ED remain poorly clarified. Rumination and psychological resilience are two promising psychological variables that may participate in this correlational pathway yet have not been empirically examined in the NRS-ED context. The present study aimed to explore the potential indirect correlational link between NRS and ED through rumination, and further evaluate whether resilience moderates this associative pathway. Between February 2024 October 2025, we conducted a cross-sectional study of 880 men with ED recruited from the Andrology Clinic of the First Affiliated Hospital of Anhui Medical University. Participants completed the NRS Scale (lower scores indicate more severe NRS), Ruminative Responses Scale, 10-item Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale, and the 5-item International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5). Pearson correlations, bootstrapped mediation, and moderated mediation models with covariate adjustment, and latent profile analysis (LPA) in Mplus were performed to identify rumination subgroups and compare erectile function across profiles. Non-restorative sleep severity was significantly associated with worse ED and elevated rumination (all P < .001). Rumination partially mediated the association between NRS and ED. Exploratory LPA identified 3 statistical patterns representing sample heterogeneity in rumination severity (low 28.86%, moderate 43.18%, high 27.96%), rather than clinically distinct phenotypes. Higher rumination severity corresponded to significantly poorer erectile function (high vs. low severity IIEF-5 scores: 8.92 ± 3.84 vs. 14.95 ± 5.03). Resilience significantly moderated this pathway, acting as a buffer that attenuated both the effect of NRS on rumination and the subsequent impact of rumination on ED. Our findings demonstrate that NRS is linked to ED via a ruminative associational pattern, and this association varies across levels of resilience. These findings suggest that integrated therapeutic strategies targeting these cognitive-emotional factors could facilitate more personalized clinical management for patients.

papers.title: Napping during major depressive episodes identifies a distinct hypersomnolence phenotype.
papers.abstract: Prior studies have linked depression with napping, though findings remain inconsistent. Given that major depressive episodes (MDE) commonly involve sleep-wake and circadian disturbances, we hypothesized that daytime Napping during MDE reflects more pronounced sleep/circadian disruptions and a distinct clinical profile. We compared MDE patients with and without napping (MDE-NAP vs MDE), as well as unipolar and bipolar subgroups, using subjective and objective biomarkers, including actigraphy. The MDE-NAP group had more frequently hypersomnia (30.6% vs 8.2% p < .001), daytime sleepiness (73.1% vs 41.8%, p < .001), daytime fatigue (97.1% vs 88.5%, p = .042), family history of depression (68.2% vs 52.2%, p = .044), weight gain (42.2% vs 21.6%, p = .006), and feelings of guilt (75.0% vs 57.8%, p = .027). The unipolar napping group had greater weight gain (48.8% vs 21.4%, p = .004) and more hypersomnia (26.1% vs 3.4%, p < .001). The bipolar napping group were more frequently women (76.9% vs 52%, p = .046), with more suicidal ideation (65.4% vs 37.8%, p = .031), sad mood (73.1% vs 43.1%, p = .019), hypersomnia (38.5% vs 15.8%, p = .04), and guilt (61.9 vs 35.1, p = .049). Regarding sleep scales, MDE-NAP had more hypersomnolence symptoms (HSI total score, p < .001), with higher frequencies of sleep inertia, daytime sleep, sleepiness, daytime dysfunction, and sleep attacks; and showed longer sleep duration (PSQI sleep duration, p = .025), and higher sleep efficiency (PSQI sleep efficiency, p = .015). Actigraphy did not reveal significant between-group differences in the subsample with usable recordings (N = 90). Daytime napping during MDE appears to identify a distinct hypersomnolence phenotype with sleep-vegetative burden, supporting the systematic assessment of napping to guide personalized sleep- and circadian-based therapeutic strategies. This paper is part of the Sleep and Circadian Mechanisms in Mental Health Collection.

papers.title: From Adiposity to Diastolic Dysfunction: The Integrated Role of Epicardial Fat, Autonomic Dysregulation, and Morning Blood Pressure Surge in Obesity.
papers.abstract: Although the association between obesity and left ventricular diastolic dysfunction (LVDD) is well established, the concurrent associations of epicardial adipose tissue (EAT), sleep-trough (prewaking) morning blood pressure surge (MBPS), and autonomic imbalance with LVDD have not been fully elucidated. This study aimed to evaluate the associations of EAT thickness, MBPS, and heart rate variability (HRV) parameters with LVDD in obese adults and to assess the cross-sectional discriminatory performance of these multimodal markers. This cross-sectional study included 240 individuals, comprising 120 obese participants (body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m2) and 120 age- and sex-matched normal-weight controls (body mass index 18.5-24.9 kg/m2). All participants underwent transthoracic echocardiography, 24-h ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, and 24-h Holter electrocardiographic analysis, with HRV data available for the entire cohort (n = 240). EAT thickness was measured echocardiographically, and LVDD was classified using contemporary guideline-based echocardiographic criteria. SDNN was predefined as the primary autonomic marker, while RMSSD and the LF/HF ratio were reported as supportive indices. Associations with LVDD (≥ Grade I) were evaluated using correlation analysis, multivariable logistic regression, and receiver operating characteristic analyses. Cross-sectional discrimination analysis and performance assessment were performed within the obese subgroup (n = 120). Compared with controls, obese participants exhibited greater EAT thickness (6.5 ± 1.7 vs. 4.0 ± 1.2 mm), higher MBPS (33 ± 10 vs. 21 ± 7 mmHg), increased LF/HF ratio, and lower SDNN and RMSSD values (all p < 0.001). The prevalence of LVDD was significantly higher in obese individuals than in controls (45% vs. 15%, p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis, EAT thickness (odds ratio [OR] = 1.20 per 1 mm; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.08-1.34), MBPS (OR = 1.35 per 10 mmHg; 95% CI 1.10-1.65), and SDNN (OR = 0.88 per 10 ms; 95% CI 0.80-0.97) were independently associated with LVDD. The parsimonious model demonstrated discrimination and calibration comparable to or superior to the full clinical model (AUC: 0.89 vs. 0.85). In obese adults, increased epicardial adiposity, exaggerated MBPS, and autonomic dysfunction coexist with LVDD. Integrated assessment of structural (EAT), hemodynamic (MBPS), and autonomic (SDNN) markers may facilitate cross-sectional identification of LVDD and improve phenotypic characterization in obesity.

papers.title: Effect of Tai Chi Exercise on Fatigue in Renal Transplant Recipients: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: Fatigue is a prevalent symptom in kidney transplant patients that not only affects quality of life but may also impact long-term graft survival. While Tai Chi has been shown to effectively reduce fatigue in patients with chronic diseases, research in kidney transplant recipients remains limited. To explore the effects of Tai Chi exercise on fatigue among kidney transplant recipients and to investigate the effectiveness and safety of Tai Chi-based rehabilitation. A prospective, single-center, parallel-arm randomized controlled trial was conducted in Northeast China. The study period for patient recruitment and intervention implementation was from 1 June 2025, to 12 October 2025. Eligible participants were kidney transplant recipients aged 18-60 years who were at least 1 month post-transplantation. Sixty-four kidney transplant patients were randomly allocated (1:1) to the intervention group (Tai Chi exercise) or the control group (routine care only). The intervention group received a 12-week Tai Chi exercise program. The primary outcome was fatigue severity assessed at 12 weeks. After 12 weeks of Tai Chi intervention, there were statistically significant differences in total fatigue scores between the two groups of renal transplant recipients. Sleep quality and 6-min walk distance were significantly improved. Tai Chi exercise is a gentle and well-tolerated exercise intervention that can effectively improve fatigue in renal transplant recipients. Trial Registration: International Traditional Medicine Clinical Trial Registry: 2026000360.

papers.title: Which Domains of Cognition in Older Adults Are Affected by Sleep Duration? A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, research on the impact of sleep duration on cognitive domains in older adults has been emerging; however, a formal synthesis of the focused literature that addresses all cognitive domains has not yet been conducted. Therefore, this review study was conducted to investigate the effects of sleep duration on various cognitive domains in older adults. This scoping review was conducted according to Arksey and O'Malley (2005). A systematic search was conducted across three research databases: PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus, with relevant gray literature also reviewed. Studies that reported on the relationship between sleep duration and cognition among older adults were included in the review. Data were extracted, charted, and synthesized into a narrative. Consistent with the purpose of a scoping review, the methodological quality of the studies was not appraised. A total of 23 studies published between 2009 and 2024 fulfilled the inclusion criteria. The findings revealed that both excessively long and short sleep durations were strongly linked to impairments in learning, memory, and complex attention. Only a limited number of studies explored all cognitive domains, with none addressing social cognition. Additionally, analyses considering gender differences were notably absent. This review highlights cognitive domains affected by inadequate sleep in older adults and emphasizes the need for more research on gender-specific differences in sleep duration. It also pointed out a gap in understanding the link between sleep duration and social cognition, emphasizing the need for further studies in this area.
